WOMEN'S CHAT.

A soft point in America.—An Indian prince appears to have got into trouble with our Transatlantic consins, because he would not admit that beauty was the divine prerogative of the American woman. She was in many ways estimable. but he astonished his interviewer by saying that as far as he could see she had no special claims to beauty. That was rather a blow to American pride, but our cousins might take comfort in the reflec- tion that the Eastern type of beauty very often differs from that of the West, and it., some countries, bulk rather than beauty of form, is looked upon as the greatest charm. On the other hand the Jackwar of Baroda, with his intimate acquaintance with European Society, may just claim to be a good judge of types of Western beauty and he has sadly disappointed our Transatlantic cousins by flatly refusing to award the I palm to the women of American. The Sperling Reform Movement.—Americans have 1 their own particular way of speaking the Anglo-Saxon language. Some of them speak it with an accent you can-lean up against and now they are going to revise I the standard rules of spelling it. to future, the Presi- dential messages, and all official documents issued from the White House, are to be spelt in accordance with the 'recommendations of the Spelling Reform Committee,of i 'which Dr. Brander Matthews s chairman, and Mr. Andrew Carnegie, and Mr. Mark Twain among the lead- Mg spirits. • Thy-ugh" will be" thru," " though" will be " tho," " mamma" will be" mama," "kissed' will be kist," and so on. Already a list of some 300 words with the unpronounced lettefs eliminated, and the " fonetic " forms substituted, has been authorised for use in the Government printing offices, and there seems little doubt that the " on "spelling will be generally adopted by the American Press and people. It may even spread to this country where the system has its advocates and opponents. So far from leading to simplicity and uniformity as President Roosevelt ex- pects, we should witness a terrible and prolonged war of words, but the issue would depend upon the attitude of the newspapers, and,if they took up the revised form we should have to have it whether we liked it or not. Stay at Home Holidays.—Undoubtedly we have developed a greater lone for our own islands and a greater wish to know more about them, for this is proving a very stay-at-home-holidayseason. Instead of tearing about the Continent, people are doing" England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales, and finding out that snch a holiday—especially if it happens to be the only one they can take in the year, is far more produc- tive of health and pleasure, than one spent in rushing about abroad. Possibly the motor has had something to do with this change in our ideas. Many people possessed of a car, are making a tour of the country by • means of it, and providing" scorching "is not indulged in, and frequent rests are taken, this particular form of holiday has much to recommend it. The Modern Landlady.—The seaside and holiday landlady used to rank with the mother-in-law as one of the most frequent objects of caricatures in the comic papers. But, with much else that has progressed with the age. so has the landlady, who caters for the family holidays of the middle classes. No doubt she has been stirred tol improve her cooking, the furnishing and appointmeats of her rooms, by the greater completion of hotels and boarding houses. But altogether she is of a better class, and a better principled person than the old fashioned landlady who was depicted as always taking toll of stores, and dishes that left the table and were expected back again, and as generally making up in abuse for her lack of attentiveness and non-fulfil- ment of obligations. No one can doubt that on the whole the modern landlady is a great improvement upon the old, and this a matter which in innumerable cases, often makes or mars the enjoyment of summer holidays. Home-Made Fabrics.—The autumn promises to find in devoted to home-made materials, Irish frieze, Scotch tweeds, English homespuns and Welsh flannels. At the moment there is quite a rush for the latter, which, by the way, differ considerably from the older types of flannel. The new varieties are of harsher make and closer resemble tweed. As regards patterns and colours they leave nothing to be desired, moreover they are delightfully light in weight. Ribbon ShoelLaces.—Coloured shoes to match the toilette are still correct but niche mode is only for the wealthy. A very good effect however, can be obtained by lacing dainty black shoes with ribbon, which can either match the gown itself, or the relieving colour. The ribbon should be as wide as possible, and tied in a neat bow. Nourishment in Plums.—The plum season is unfor- tunately a failure, this year, although no doubt we shall receive pleas of supplies from abroad. The scarcity in our borne orchards is nevertheless to be regretted because we are told that there is more invigorating force in fresh plums than in almost any other kind of fruit. Consequent upon some recent scientific analysis it appears that plume, like bananas, ace rich in nitrogen, and it is deduced that one may get five times the amount of energy from a pound of fresh plums, that is available from a pound of fresh strawberries. Dreams.—The correspondence on dreams and visions which is one of the silly season subjects of a great London paper, recalls to mind the story related in his autobugrsphy 'by Mr. Locker-Lampson, of the dream of Halle's cook. She had won a good sum in a lottery with the number twenty-three, and Hall, being glad to hear of her good fortune inquired how she happened to fix on so lucky a number. "I had a dream, sir,' she said, " I dreamt of number seven—l dreamt of it three times, and as " three times seven makes twenty-three, I chose that number."—lt is said that it is better to be 'born lucky than rich, and evidently this woman's luck triumphed over her arithmetic.
INIADGE.

div.head: Sad Burning Fatality.
div.p: Sad Burning Fatality.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at Warrington on Monday on the body of Theresa Burke, who died in the Infirmary on Friday as the result of burns sustained earlier in the week. Annie Burke, wife of James Burke, 9, James-greet, said the deceased was three years and nine months of age. On the morning of the 21st August witness was called to a neighbour's house to see to a woman who was ill. Her daughter at the time was playing in the street. Shortly afterwards she was imformed that deceased was on fire and she went and put out the flames with a rough apron which she was wearing. On going into the house she found some pieces of burnt paper and was of opinion that her daughter had been play- ing with the fire. Tnere was nh one in the house at the time. Nurse Crowther stated that deceased, when admitted to the Infirmary, was suffering from severe burns about the arms and face.—A verdict of " Accident death" was raurned.

BLACKPOOL'S CHIEF CONSTABLESHTP. Mr.Derham,Chief Constable of Blackpool,has for some time been eligible for a pension, but he wishes to , remain at work, and the Watch Committee have decided \ to retain his services under the new Police Superannua- tion Act. He is to have a house rent free.

div.head: STOCKT9N HEATH PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.
div.p: STOCKT9N HEATH PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.
Mr. Hallows and jar. Whitley.

- -- The monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee was held at the Hall Cafe on Tuesday even- ing when there were present 1 Messrs. G. Pilling (in the chair) J. Whitley, J. Hallows, S. F. Welsby, F. Pearson, W. Mclntyre, J. H. Clarke, T. Williams, F. Warburton, J. W. Bouchier, G. F. Ashton (clerk), and J. Swinton (surveyor)..... .

.GOAIPI.AIi7T ABOUT DANCING. Mr. Pearson said he had received several complaints about the dancing at the Hall L'af4 which was carried on in season and out of season. Be would like to know whether the committee considered it necessary or advisable that they should apply for powers to regulate the dancing. Mr. Hallows gave notice that he would move that the Parochial Committee adopt the Towns Police Clauses Act to enable them to deal with the complaints.

div.head: RECENT FIRS.
div.p: THE RECENT FIRS.

' Mr. Warburton' chairman of the Fire Brigade Com- mittee, said that at last the Brigade had justified its , existence by the promptitude with vvbich it was on the! ' scene on the occasion of the recent fire in Grappenhall- road. Mr. Hallows suggested that there should be a better arrangement for summoning the firemen. At present I they bad to be personally called from all over the village with the result that they put in an appearance one by one. Mr. Clarke thought that what transpired at the fire justified the expense which the committee had incurred in providing fire appliances. It was felt that some better means should be devised for summoning the men and that more frequent practices should be held. The matter was however left in the bands of Mr. Warburton. A COMPLAINT YROM MR. HALLOWS. Mr. Hallows said that at the last meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council Mr. Whitley gave the L Council to understand that he had been asked by several members of the Committee to bring forward the ques- tion of a finger pose in Walton-road. He would like to I know a which meeting of the Committee the matter was mentioned, as he could not remember it having , been brought forward. He )lad attende,cl all public meetings of the Committee, but no private ones. Mr. Whitley : I was asked to bring the matter for- ward at Dutton. Mr. Hallows : I don't object to my friend bringing questions forward, but he ought first of all to bring them before this Committee. 'dr. Whitley: I was only doing what thought was my duty. Whether a matter comes before this Com- mittee or not it is my duty to look after the ratepayers. Mr. Hallows : My only objection is that it should have come before this Committee first.

div.head: TREE PLANTING.
div.p: TREE PLANTING.

Mr. Clarke said he saw that the Highways Committee of the District Council proposed, at a later date, to visit Stockton Heath to consider which of the trees that had been planted in the village had to be removed. He quite agreed that certain of the trees were a nuis- ance and dangerous. He would, however, like to suggest that when the Committee did visit Stockton Heath they should allow representatives of the Parochial Committee and the Tree Planting Committee to meet them. Mr. Pilling said that doubtless that would be done.

SERIOUS MILL FIRE. A serious fire broke out at about midnight on Monday at the Brookside Mill, Newton-le-Willows, occupied by Mr. S. Boardman, flour and corn biller. Messrs. M'Corquodale and Company's fire brigade and the Urban Council brigade got promptly to work, but the fire burned so fiercely that it was not until daybreak that the brigales were able to leave. Tbe damage done was serious, as the premises were gutted. The surrounding property was saved. The origin of the fire is not known.

DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
LADY MASTER OF AOLNDS.

The Marchioness of Graham, the daughter of the late Duke of Hamilton, is a M.o.H. who is looking forward to being with her hounds again.' Little wonder is it she is so keen in matters venatic, says 4110 e Gentleiroman, for in her Lady- ,ship's case, as in most others of the sex feminine who take an active part in hunting, an heredi- tary love of everything appertaining to the chase was born with her. Another lady at the head of bounds is Miss Kate Rose-Cleland, who presides over the interests of the Rathgall pack, and was a short time ago presented with six couples of nineteen-inch pure-bred harriers by local friends in recognition of the sport she and her sister have shewn, and in hope of still further improv- ing it in the coming season. One of the most famous lady sportswomen is the Duchess of New- castle,' who hunts the Clamber Harriers, which are her own property. Her country is chiefly within the territory of Lord Galway's and the Rufford Hounds. The Duchess started the pack in 1895, and now has some twenty couples of hounds. Her Grace is as well known with fox- hounds as harriers, and is a perfect horsewoman. So far as hound lore goes, Mrs. Pryse-Rice, who owns a pack of harriers in South Wales, is al- most equally famous. A PINAFORE FROCK. •

The pinafore frock has been much in vogue during the summer months, and has been for the most part exploited in linen, print, and even muslin; but there is no reason why so charming a model should be allowed to pass away with the hot weather, and our accompanying sketch shows what can be accomplished on pinafore lines for autumn wear. A mauve and white check tweed has been chosen for the main part of the dross. AT the very hour and minute when we described Arthur Esmond as perhaps the happiegt man on earth, that is to say, at three o'clock in the afternoon on the day of the robbery, at this moment perhaps one of the most miserable men in London was Mr. Robert Marcas. Mr. Marcas was a man of some fifty years, thin, sallow, with a cat-like moustache and a furtive manner. He had been a solicitor till the Incorporated Law Society had struck, him off the rolls for nefarious practices, and now for two years he had been "living on his wits." He looked thin enough on this regime and ragged enough. He had fallen as only a bad man can fall, for he had not one friend in the world or a person who would trust him with a shilling. , As a solicitor. he had practised entirely for the criminal classes, and he had possessed a large clientele amongst the thieves and rogues of London, he was up to every .trick of the trade as far as robbery was Concerned : in fact, kthere was little of evil in this world that Mr. Robert Mamas was not up to. On the day upon which this story opened Mr. Marcas_ had received peremptory notice I from his landlady that he must pay his bill or ' vacate his rooms . that evening. He had not breakfasted, and, worse than all, his stock of cigarettes had given out. He had pawned everything pawnable, and as he walked down High Street, Notting Hill, at two in the after- noon of this. momentous day he was literally' and absolutely penniless. , Half-past three found him at Holland Park where he had been trying to borrow some money unsuccessfully from an acquaintance 1.. in the public-house line. He was nearing the Tube Station when sud- denly before him he saw a figure walking quickly and carrying a bag. Mr. Maros had an eye that never forgot a face, or a figure, or a manner, or a gesture, or a voice, or arry thing at all that would serve for the identification of a person. , He quickened his race and' followed the figure that had attracted his attention. It was a somewhat remarkable figure that Vr. Marcas was fol:owitig, that of a person ~vpssed in 'very antiquated clothes of country WO an old man with a benign expression of :ountenance, a second edition of the Vicar of Wake:ield, in fact, carrying a handbag which no doubt contained his next Sunday's sermon and a few toilet necessaries for a stay of a day or two in London. As he hobbled along at a very swift pace ;4.3:;pite his years and apparent infirmities he qazed about him •witti a wandering • and amazed , expression astounded ' apparently by the newness.of the scene around him. Mr. Marcas chuckled to himself as he fol- lowed .the benign joolsin,g old gentleman who was making in the direction ofi Notting Hill Gate.

" Oxford man, sir," said the Gratter. "Education, why what do you take me for? Of course, I'm a man of education, else how could I work my plans as I do. The ordinary man who lives by his wits fails simply from want of education. Mind, my dear sir, will always triumph over matter. But here we are at the 'Plume of Feathers.'" The "Plume of Feathers" was a small public-house situated in a back street off High Street, Notting Hill Gate, They entered the bar where several men were drinking and passed on into a back parlour, the Grafter leading the way and walking with an assur- ance that made it evident he was not a stranger to the place. They took their seats at a round table in the centre of which stood a pyramid of wax fruits under a dusty glass case. The Grafter rapped on the table and the landlord entered. He was a big, burly, brutal-looking man, who seemed to have lived on beer from his earliest youth. pounds worth, and you give me a paltry ten pounds and a bag that's enough evidence itself to hang a man." " Your life ain't worth tuppence," said the Grafter. "It's putting a premium on crime to give you ten pounds to help you to live; it's one of the worst deeds I've ever done, and if you say another word I'll take the money back."

Marcas hastily put the ten sovereigns in his pocket. "I'll be even with you yet," he muttered "No threats," said the Grafter. "You're wasting your breath. I'm not afraid of you. You know me to-day because I' am in the same get up as when you last saw me. After to- day I shall use this disguise no more. Now, adieu, my dear boy, and good luc " He opened the door, went out,l and shut it after him, leaving Marcas seated t the table before the empty bag. Outside in tne Dar tne Graftk nodded to the landlord, tossed him a sovereign, and without waiting for the change went into the street.
A hansom cab was at the corner; he entered it and ordered the driver to take him to Wardour Street.

As he drove !,lie smiled to himself at the use he had ;put Marcas to. Marcas had turned up in fact ;most opportunely, for a bag is a very difficult thing to get rid of. You cannot put it in your pocket, and at every attempt you hiake to dispose of it you leave a trace. He had not the least fear of Marcus splitting or givin,g information as to what he had told him. He knew Marcas well, and knew facts about his ilife that gave him a powerful hold upon him. At the top of Wardour Street he got out and paid his driver liberally, then he walked down Wardour Street and turned into Old Compton Street.

Old Compton Street is perhaps the centre of foreign life in Soho. Here you can buy macaroni from Naples, Bologna sausages straight from Bologna, Italian and Spanish cigarettes, French novels, newspapers, and foreign literature generally. Nearly every shop is kept by a foreigner, and nearly every foreigner seems to be an Italian. At a certain shop in Soho the Grafter stopped and drawing a key from his pocket, entered at a side door.

He shut the door and passing up the stairs reached a door on the first landing; opening it with a curiously shaped key, he entered a mlast cosy and comfortable furnished room. A fire was bur ins on the- hearth, and on the hob stood a kettle. The paper and upholstery of the apartment was in a deep red tone; there were no picthres, but numerous books. Against one wall stood a piece of furniture shaped like a closed bookcase. He opened the oaken doors.' The interior was fitted not with shelves and books, but with small racks holding or supporting all sorts of strange-look- ing instruments. Pinchers and files, minia- ture saws, centre bits, plyers, were there all. polished and shining as a surgeon's instru- ments when laid on the table before an opera- tion. There was also a complete oxyhydro- gen blow pipe on a small scale beautifully made adaptable to the pocket and capable, from the awful intensity of its flame, to burn out any lock in Christendom. There was a small X-ray apparatus, a long row of little bottles filled with various coloured chemicals, test tubes, litmus paper, and all the stock-in- trade of the analytical chemist. It was evident that the Grafter carried on his business in the most modern way, that whatever his morals or manners might be in his profession he was facile princeps and , thoroughly up-to-date. He opened a drawer in this depository, put into it the opal,' the jewels, and the papers he had taken from the bag. Then he closed and locked the bureau, made himself a cup of tea, and taking a seat in an armchair by the fire drew forth the paper covered with cypher .writing which he had taken from the bag. " Now for this," said he to himself, settling himself comfortably in his chair. The Grafter, whatever else he might be, was no doubt a mathematician of a high order, that is to say, not a mere calculator, but a man who used the powers of mathematical analysis and synthesis in dealing ndt only with rows of figures, but with every day affairs. He sat with the cypher writing in his hand for an hour. testing it by all the processes 'known to his ingenuity. It resisted them all. Theh he came to the conclusion that 'he was dealing with a cypher never invented before, an extraordinary cypher guarding, no doubt, an extraordinary secret.
Then he left the armchair, went to the table, and set to work in earnest.

It was midnight when, exhausted and haggard, the Grafter finished. He had wrested the secret from the crypto- gram, a secret so immense, so fraught with eventualities, that despite his satisfaction at his own success, a feeling of uneasiness came over him and possessed him for perhaps the first time in his life.
(To .be continued.)

div.head: LOCAL PREACHER'S EVIDENCE.
div.p: LOCAL PREACHER'S EVIDENCE.
Zam-Buk ends Terrible Suffering
from Piles.

Mr. Joshua Nicholson, of 68, Poplar-street, South Moor, is one of the best known lay preachers in Durham, and an active member of the Zion Primitive Methodist Church. The words xhich he has recently spoken in honest gratitude to Zam-Buk must rank as evidence of unusual weight. To a " Durham Chronicle " reporter he said :—" I was attacked by piles about six and a half /ears ago. I attributed it to draughts, cold, and sweating whilst following my daily occupation in the mine. Some- times I went to work in the morning feeling in any usual state of health, and before the shift was flnishea I could hardly bear up. " The piles often bled, and occasionally there was a discharge of mucus from the irritated membranes. I suffered intense pain and irritation. I have many times ' worked, or sat preparing for my Sunday engagements,ia the greatest agony, and sometimes I really did not know how I would be able to preach or work at all. After a service I was quite done up. I lost much sleep, and occasionally had to stay away from work. "I tried a French ointment and other medicines, but did not notice any good result. It was the same with the prescriptions of two doctcas' and their ointments were quite useless. Nothing my friends recommended me seemed to do any good. Both doctors agreed that I would have to undergo an operation, but I objected. " I was never free for any length of time during the six years and a half I suffered. At lengtha friend showed me a book about Zam-Buk, and seeing a case like mine mentioned I gave the balm a trial. I found it. most soothing and cooling, and it soon began to reduce the swellings. After the first box I felt a lot better, and continued dressings set me on my feet again. lam now perfectly and permanently cured, solely by the use of Zam-Buk.'

div.head: GERMAN ERROR.
div.p: A GERMAN ERROR.
South Lancashlres Unjustly Accused of
Cowardice.

Great indignation has been occasioned in the ranks of the South Lancashire Regiment by the issue of the German official history of the War in South Africa, in which they are accused—unjustly accused—of gross cowardice. On page 259, describing the events of ,February 23rd (the Pieter's Hill engagement), the history says :—*` This firing, which suddenly broke out with great violence, threw the South Lancashires on the right flank into such a state of alarm that they too rushed pell-mell down the hill in full flight. Their leaders had completely lost control over the terrified mass." Colonel R. H. Hall, who at the time was assist- ing in command, has written to the Army Council saying " I beg most emphatically to contradict this statement. No such thing ever happened to the South Lanes- shires. I was second in command of the battalion at the time, and during the previous night (22-23) had entrenched and occupied Green Hill with four com- panies, holding this position until relieved by the Doyens at dusk on February 23. As General Wynne, who commanded the 11th Ilrigate, was wounded early on February 22, and as his successor, General W. Kitchener, did not, I believe, take up the command of the brigade until February 24, I cannot refer to either of these general officers to refute the mis-statement, but I believe that General Sir Charles Warren, who conducted the attack on Wynne Hill, would be able to do so, and thus do justice to the South Lancashire Regiment, who, I know, will bitterly resent this unjust accusation. I would also refer to the three senior officers now serving who were present at Wynne Hill and Green Hill, viz., Major Upperton, Captain Green, and Captain Oakeley, who, I feel confident will fully corroborate me in my assertion that the statement quoted is absolutely untrue, so far as the South Lanca- shire Regiment is concerned." The officers at Orford Barracks are highly incensed at the reflection which is cast upon the honour of the Regiment and strongly support Colonel Hall in his emphatic denial of the charge.

• FURTHER DENIALS. Writing to the e Manchester Evening News," one who signs himself " Cler et Audex " says :—" As. one who was at Green Hill, and also at all engagements up /o Pieters Hill, I can most emphati- cally endorse all the statements made by Colonel Hall. I followed the Lancashire Brigade from Frere upwards, and the statement is a gross libel upon them. At Green Hill, it ii true, a few men were disconcerted by a shell maiming one or two of their comrades (this company being slightly in advance of the Howitzer Battery. R.A.), but they never budged one inch. I might add that the brigade and divisional headquarters were immediately on the right overlooking the Tugela. Possibly Colonel Hall will remember the Composite Rifle Battalion, who showed that as Reservists they had not forgotten ,their previous tuition. Ctssar's Hill, Green Hill. and/ Pieters Hill engegemeuts seem to have been treated sjightingly bycorrespondents, but the fact remains, nevertheless, that through these engagements Ladysmith was relieved at last. Let no one (German or otherwise) dare cast a slur on the Lancashire Brigade or any detail of it. They, in common with all under Buller, performed an arduous tash, and as one who was. present throughout, I only feel It my, duty to resent. such gross slanders." Mr. W. S. Harper writes to the "Manchester Guardian :—" As an eye-witness of the incident described by the German historian I as that such did not take place in the ranks of the South Lancashires' but in the regiment on their immediate left on that occasion. Rather than allow the stigma to rest on the innocent the truth should be spoken. lam almost certain that ESOMO of the divisional staff ofiloers helped to rally the waverer; and they should rectify the error.

Four days after the above-mentioned occurrence the battle of 'Platers Hill was fought, and, to quote from General Buller's despatch, "the position was magnifi- cently carried by the South Lencashires about sunset." The feeding illustrated papers,however,and the publica- tion, " With the flag to Pretoria," depict a totally different regiment "carrying the position," Genera Warren expressed his opinion that the work of Oa South Lancashire Regiment during the Boer war has ot been truly recorded."

An inquest was held on Monday at Warrington .by Ur. S. Brighouse into the circuvastances of a drowning fatality which °centred in the Manchester Ship Canal. at Latchford on Friday.— It appears that Thomas Lloyd and a companion, Herbert Bratendale, 26. Thelwnil lane, attended the Wash lane school, and after being released from their studies on Friday afternoon went to gather blackberries on the banks of the Manchester Ship Canal. They observed a bottle floating in the water and in trying to teach it deceased overbalanced and fell into the water. Brazendale made several ineffectual attempts to reach him but itri.s not aisle to do so. Deceased's father assisted to recover the body later in the evening. Captain Waring, on behalf of the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany shid the lads were trespassing and the spot where they were was a very dangerous one. He had fre- quently warned boys about being on the canal banks and had sent them away. He expressed his sympathy with the parents of the deceased.—A verdict of "Accidental death "was returned.

MAN-HUNTING IN CHURCH WITH A REVOLVER. Man hunting in church with a revolver during Divine service is more than a little unusual. This, however, has happened at Altrincham, where a young lady, after examining the congregation, told the apparitor that she had a revolver and intended to use it to the detriment of a gentleman present. The latter escaped by the vestry and was pursued by the lady, fruitlessly, to his house.

THE BLACK SANDS OF THE PACIFIC. It is estimated that there is enough magnetite in the black sands of the Pacific coast to supply all the iron and steel required on the western seaboard. Much of the sand also contains zircon, which is worth £4O ato Sonic samples,, again, run high in monazite, which is in request for the making of incandescent gas mantles. The machines by which the ore is concentrated may •be described as quivering tables over which pour perpetual streams of water. These have grooved surfaces by means of which the heavier and valu- able parts are collected together, and the rest washed away. •

div.head: TIDAL *LAKE.
div.p: A TIDAL *LAKE.

Lakes and inland seas, such as the Baltic and the Euxine, have always been considered outside the tide-producing effect of the lunar attraction, but the investigations of Professor Loudon, of Toronto University, into the periodical oscilla- tions of Lake Huron will somewhat modify that theory. Impressed with the regularity—more especially in calm weather—of the general out- line of the movements, the Professor entered minutely into the matter, and ascertained a well- marked rise and fall twice a day, no oscillation exceeding four hours. These facts, which later investigation amply verified, leave little room for doubt that on one at least of the five great lakes separating Canada from the United States a true lunar tide occurs.
• THE COLOUR OF WATER.

It was long ago discovered that the natural colour of water is blue, and not white, as most of us usually supposed. Opinions have not agreed on the cause of • the green and yellow tints; these, it has been discovered by W. Spring, are due to extraneous substances. Dis- solved calcium salts, though apparently giving a green tint, duo to a fine invisible suspension, have no effect on the colour of water when ade- quate precautions are taken. The brown or yellow colour due to iron salts is not seen when calcium is present. The green tint is often due to a condition of equilibrium between the colour- effect of the iron salts and the precipitating aO- - of the calcium salts

, ALLOYS OF CALCIUM. In Veraiturgie, L. Stockem describes experi- illints Which demonstrate that calcium cannot be ,a4LoYed with iron, the introduction of calcium into molten pig-iron, and into iron reduced by Al, failing to produce an alloy and onry result- ing in a slight decarburisation of the pig-iron. Iron oxide can be reduceri,by calcium, and forma ductile beads of iron free from Ca, even when a, large excess of Ca is used. Calcium-copper alloys are readily formed by pouring molten Cu into a magnesia-lined crucible containing fragments of Ca. Even small additions of Ca make copper brittle, an alloy containing 7 per cent. Ca being so brittle that bars five centimetres thick can be broken by light taps with a hammer. The alloy containing 20 per cent. Ca is white, and decom- poses in air.

div.head: AN INGENIOUS BEACON.
div.p: AN INGENIOUS BEACON.

On a sunk reef 350 ft. distant from Stornoway Lighthouse is a remarkable beacon, which warns mariners with the help of a light which is only apparent. The beacon is a cone of cast-iron plates, surmounted with a lantern containing a glass prism. This prism derives its light from refracting the rays emitted from the lighthouse, and the optical delusion is marvellous. Mariners naturally suppose that there is a lighted lamp on the beacon itself, and many of them will not be- lieve otherwise. But the object of the beacon is attained when the navigator sees the reflected light, which indicates the perilous rock below. This beacon in the north of Scotland has been in _

nee more than half a century, and since it wa fixed in position others have been placed in other neighbourhoods to make clear points of danger. It is an ingenious and very effective safeguard against perils of the coast.

ANIMALS' DEATH RESORTS. The curious habit of the Guanacos of South America of resorting to one particular spot to lay down their bones when death overtakes them has often been commented on by natural- ists. "They seem also to have favourite locali- ties in which to die, as appears from the great heaps of bones, bearing no signs of having been gnawed by the puma, which have been found in particular spots," as one writer tells us. And on the shores of the lake "lay per- fact 'skeletons of scores of dead yak. All seemed to choose the shores of this wonderful lake to die by." Lieutenant Armitage, in his "Two Years in the Antarctic," notices a similar habit on the part of the crab-eating seal. During a sledge journey westwards from the Discovery's winter questers, near Mount Erebus, they came across carcases of this animal at a height of 2,000 ft. or 3,000 ft. above sea level, and thirty miles from the coastline. "The seal," writes Lieutenant Armitage, "apparently knowing of its approach- ing dissolution, crawls painfully and wearily up, sal ever upwards, until death overtakes it"

div.head: NITROGEN IN FRUIT.
div.p: NITROGEN IN FRUIT.

Some very important analyses have been com- pleted which shew the percentages of nitrogen oontained in the various fruits. The experimenters admit that the results are remarkable. Of the fresh fruits dealt With, it was found that persim- mons contained the largest proportion, the per- centage being 297; bananas came second with 21'0. The rest were as follows: Pomegranates, 168; cherries, 16.5; pears, 15-7; grapes, 149; apples, 13'0; whortleberries, 10'3; raspberries, 9'7; pineapples, 9.3; blackberries, 8.4; cran- berries, B'4; lemons, 7.4; melons, 7'2; straw- berries, 6'o; peaches, s'B; olives, 5.7. Several other fruits were dealt with, but in their cases the total percentages of nitrogefi and crude fibre were included together. These vary- ing percentages were as follows: Plums, 201; prunes, 189; figs, 188; huckleberries, 16'6; nec- tarines, 159; apricots, 134; currants, 128; oranges, 116; water-melons, 6'7; avocados, 6.8. The whole of these figures refer to fresh fruits. There can be no doubt that the larger percent- ages of nitrogen contained in persimmons and bananas have had more to d97with their inciess- ing popularity than has heretofore been imagined.

div.head: CLIMATE AND ALCOHOL.
div.p: CLIMATE AND ALCOHOL.

It is generally believed that the consumption of alcohol, especially in concentrated forms, is greatest in cold climates, and that its effects are there less harmful, owing to more rapid oxida- tion and the more active life of the natives, while the neglect to reduce the amount of aleohol in warmer regions is considered one of thre chief causes of disease among Europeans in the tropics. The researches of Dr. Sikorsky, of Kief, seem to shew that this is far from the truth. His country 'is admirably suited for such in investigation, for over a vast extent of lati- tide from the White Sea to the Caucasus the tus.sitin peasant has for generations been testing the effects of his favourite solution of alcohol (vodka) with a vigour and persistency worthy of a martyr of science. According to official statistics, the north Russian drinks from 246 to 3-07 litres absolute alcohol per annum, while his brother in the south imbibes no less than 3•5 to 4.8 litres. Yet the deaths from alcoholism shew a regular increase northward. being 15 to 22 to the 1.000,000 in south, 40 in the centre, and 70 to 110 in north Russia. Moreover, there is a marked increase of such deaths in specially sold years. Dr. Sikorsky concludes that cold greatly in- creases, even to threefold, the toxicity of alcohol, which, as is well known, so far from increasing bodily temperature, acts as a decided antithernuo by paralysing the peripheral vessels and diminish- ing organic metabolism.

div.head: TIIE ACTION OF RADIUM ON GEMS.
div.p: TIIE ACTION OF RADIUM ON GEMS.

A. Miethe, the author of a paper on the coloration of gems by radium rays, published in Ann. d. Phrik, studied the action of these rays on a large number of gems, and fcund that many of them are influenced by the rays. No general principles can be indicated, except that the more transparent gems shew a greater tendency towards coloration than the opaque or highly coloured ones. Miethe used a pre- paration of 60 milligrammes of radium bromide. A colourless diamond from Borneo was coloured a light yellow after eight days, and a decided lemon-yellow after another eight days. On heat- ing the diamond to 250deg.C. the yellow colour was diminished, but it could not be entirely got rid ,of even at a red heat. A colourless Brazil diamond shewed no coloration. A peculiar be- laviour was shown by a pale blue sapphire from Ceylon. After only two hours' exposure to radium bromide it shewed a coloration, green at first, then light yellow, and after a few more urs reddish yellow. After a fortnight it was a dark yellow approaching chestnut. The colour muld be got rid of by heating, but' the light yellow colour always returned on cooling. Rubies ahew no change. and tinted tourmalines very little. div.head: Examiner, Saturday, September 1, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, September 1, 1906.

took all his presence of mind to conceal. °I will save that girl from this woman," he had said to himself with decision. The question now was, how to proceed. Should he try to snatch a few words with her in going ashore, or should he write? He then remembered that he did not know where to address a letter, and the matter I‘as immediate. After turning things over in his mind for some time he decided to write a short note and trust to the chance of finding an oppor- tunity of delivering it himself. He tore a leaf from his pocket-book, and after making several attempts to express his meaning wrote the following words:

"You are in much danger. I fear you are deceived in the lady with whom you are travel- ling. I greatly desire to have a few words with you to explain my meaning. Can you forgive me, an utter stranger, for taking this liberty?" - -

He signed his name and gave his address in Paris, then folded the paper into small compass and put it into his pocket. Fortune gave him his opportunity soon after they reached Paris. He was in the Custom House, undergoing the examination of his luggage, when he found him- self close to the two ladies. He felt like a thief, trying to escape observation, as he endeavoured to give the note to Sybil Hammond. She took it from him almost unconsciously, then, perceiving what she had done, drew herself up with pridt., looked him full in the free, dropped the note at his feet, turned her back upon him, and engaged herself in conversation with Miranda.

John felt mortified. The col_9ur mounted to his bronzed face as he turned aside. He was foiled for the moment, but his quick wit at once perceived another plan. He would follow their cab. He had learnt one thing at any rate —her name. He had seen it neatly engraved upon her small hand-bag. Through all his annoyance he felt pleased that the girl had behaved as she had. "It is exactly how she ought to have turned upon a strange man," he said; and yet he was vexed that circumstances had placed him in this particularly uncomfortable and false position. Leaving his luggage to be sent on to his hotel he stepped into a cab just as Mrs. Lister and her companion were leaving the station. He told his man to follow at a distance, but to keep the first cab in sight the whole time. After a drive of some length they finally stopped at a house in the Champs Elys6es, and he at once gave instructions to be driven past. Keeping himself well back in his seat to escape 'observation he carefully noticed the house and the number, making a note of the latter in his book. He then told his man to drive to the Continental. There was nothing more to be done that night, so he went in and dined. The two ladies entered the charming apart. ments which looked so dainty and fresh. Miranda seemed perfectly at home as she threw off her heavy travelling wraps. "I thought you would like my little flat," she said, delighted at Svbil's admiration. "Welcome to Paris, dear, and may you have a real good time here. May We both have," she added, playfully. "I am simply iharmed with it," returned Sybil; "and I am sure it will be my own fault if Ido not have a. good time. You are too kind. This is not at ad the sort of thing I expected when I came out as a companion." "Please forget the horrid word, and fancy you are my sister or something. I should like you to call me by my Christian name, too, if _ you have no objections." Sybil felt that she had fallen upon' a bed of roses. She went to sleep that night imagining all kinds of delightful things in the future. John Thornley had crossed her mind several times, but whenever she had thought of him she had felt hot and displeased. "How could I be so deceived in a man? I could have staked my faith upon his being a gentleman. And what must he have thought of me to assume he could take such a liberty ? " Curiously, she never mentioned the incident to Miranda. She was up early next morning. She slipped on her dressing-gown and flung open her window. It was a bright, exhilarating morning, with hardly a cloud to be seen. How delightful and strange it all felt! She seemed to be in a new world. Everything had interest for her, even to the smallest detail. How clean and bright things looked after the grime and dirt of London! The houses on the opposite side to her stood out in strong relief against the bright blue sky. The sunshine brought out the deep reds and yellows of the autumn leaves and gleamed upon the white fronts of the buildings. She was delighted, and she turned away with tears of joy in her lovely eyes. Just then she heard a knock at the door, and; to her "Come in," Morton entered. She brought a message from Miranda. Would Miss I Hammond be ready to drive with Madame at I ten o'clock. An hour later she and Mrs. Lister were sitting behind a pair of lovely greys in a perfectly appointed victoria. "I have a little shopping to get through first," said Miranda, "and then we go on to lunch with friends."

Sybil was rather astonished at Miranda's appearance this morning. She did not seem quite the same as hitherto. Her costume was more pronounced, the colour in her cheeks a little deeper, and there was generally a more festive air about her. After two hours spent in choosing most costly clothing of various kinds which she fancied she required, she gave .the order to be driven to the house of the friends with whom they were to lunch. A large over. dressed woman received them with great effusive- ness, making much of Sybil. There were several gentlemen in the room, but no other ladies. They were introduced to Sybil, and she made herself agreeable as well as her limited French would allow. She talked with them some little time whilst Mimnda was still occupied with their hostess. Somehow, she was very uncomfortable in their society. There was nothing very definite that she could object to in what they said, but it was the tone and expression that accompanied their words that annoyed her—particularly in the case of one man. She found herself wondering whether all Frenchmen were like these, and mentally comparing them to the man with whom she had travelled from London to Dover, though she was displeased with herself when she dis- covered the trend of her thoughts. By the time they left in the middle of the afternoon the feel- ing had increased greatly. The conversation, to say the least of it, had lacked refinement; and although she had not been able to follow all that was said she had understood sufficient to fully realise that these people lived upon a lower plane than those with whom she had hitherto associated. Her astonishment was in Miranda. She seemed to join in and take everything as a matter of course. She appeared quite happy in the company of these people. "You will all be at my 'At Home' to-morrow evening," she said, lightly, as they left, and Sybil wondered still more. Mrs. Lister noticed that she was rather quiet as they drove home. "I hope you have enjoyed your day, dear ? " she said, as they neared the Champs Elysees. "How did you like my French friends? ' "Not particularly, I am sorry to say," returned Sybil, timidly. 'Oh, my child, all that is insular proludice. You will think of things in quite a different light in six weeks'. time." .

-"Heaven grant that I may not!" WU the girl's mental ejaculation. She was glad to be once more alone in her room. She found there a letter addressed to herself, having the Paris post-mark upon it. "Who can possibly know me in Paris ? " she said, as she tore open the envelope. She unfolded the letter and read almost the same words written in the note she had thrown upon the floor of the Paris Custom House only the previous day. Had she received this letter only a few hours earlier she would have destroyed and taken no further notice of it. But now, read in the light of the day's experience, she gave it thoughtful attention. "At any rate I will see him," she decided at length, after much pondering. "I will ask him to call here to- morrow evening. There can be no harm in that, and it will give me time for consideration." She wrote a precise little note to John Thornley, saying that she would grant him the interview he wished for, though she had not the slightest idea of his meaning. She said that nine o'clock the following evening would be the best time for him to call. She fixed this hour as Miranda would then be engaged with her guests, and she hoped to be able to slip from the room un- observed. _ _

The following day was occupied by Mrs. Lister in attending to various small matters. Sybil's time was spent in pronouncing opinion upon first one costume, and then another. 'which Miranda put on Tor her inspection, and in arranging the masses of flowers which had been ordered, regard- less of cost, for the decoration of the salon. She loved her work, as far as the flowers were concerned, and arranged them with exquisite Lute, but there were far too many—an extrava- gant profusion which grieved her. The scent, too, was overpowering, though the room was

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
"WANTED-A COMPANION.'
By SHIRLEY RAYNARD,
Author of "Robert Lanyon's Mistake," "The Opal Ring," "The Turn of the Tide," "Madge of the Manse," "A Thorn in the Tyre," &e.

"Yes,: it is quite certain I must have a companion," said Miranda Lister to herself, musingly, as she lay back in a capacious easy- chair before the fire of a hotel sitting-room. She reached a blotting-pad from the table, drew a jewelled pencil-case from her chain, and began to draft an advertisement After spending some time, and using several sheets of paper, she apparently satisfied herself. She made a fair copy of her final effort, enclosed it in an envelope, rang the bell, and ordered its posting at once. The advertheement she sent ran thus:

"Wanted. —A young lady about twenty-five years of age, as travelling companion. Good salary and expenses to suitable person. An interview necessary." When the boy had taken away the note Miranda seemed as if a load had been lifted from her mind. The languid air she had worn for some time gave place to brisk movement She walked about the room putting in place her scattered belongings, gate a touch to the flowers upon the table, poked up the fire, and finally decided she would go out and shop. She went to her room and put on a becoming costume, then ordered a hansom and drove to Bond-street. Next morning Mrs. Lister took her breakfast in bed. She more often did so than not, as she said it gave her time to make her plans for the day without interruption. Her maid, having folded a dainty wrapper round her shoulders and arranged her breakfast-tray, had gone down to fetch the letters. After an absence of a few minutes she returned with a pile of envelopes of various shapes and sizes, which she brought to her mistress., '

"Thank you Morton.° said she; "put them down. I shall not wail', you again for an hour." The maid lingered temoment over some trifling arrangements, hoping to read something from her mistress's face of the matter in hand; but finding that Miranda had no intention of taking her in any way into her confidence, she quietly retired.

Miranda took up the letters and opened them one after another, until she had gone through the pile. She then chose out six and put them on one side, whilst she tore up the remainder into small pieces—"too small," she said to herself, "for even Morton to piece together." Later she wrote noteeto the writers of the six letters -.Acing them to call upon her the following day• line then rang the bell for her maid and proceeded with her toilet.

The six applicants called at the appointed times next morning. The first two who arrived Miranda made short work of, telling them at enee that they were unsuitable and were too old. They turned Away sadly, feeling crushed; and walked down the broad .staircase of the hotel with weary footsteps and tears in their eyes, wondering where they should turn next. The third who arrived was of an entirely different stamp from the first two. She was young, good- looking, and well dressed, and had a general air of good breeding. "She'll do," Miranda mentally congratulated herself before she had been in conversation with her five minutes. Sybil Hammond was engaged, and was to enter upon her duties almost immediately. The other three applicants Miranda refused to see. ,Having obtained her object the affairs of other people were of no account to her.

This was Sybil Hammond's first engagement, and she felt hei self fortunate in having obtained it so easily. Things had been going badly at some for the last year or two, and she had decided to relieve her parents of her maintenance— for a time at least. She had led a somewhat sheltered life in the country, some thirty miles from London. As the daughter of a professional man, she had always moved in the best society the small town could provide. Mn. Lister had weighed well in her mind as to whether she would be able to hoodwink 4 girl of this stamp, but she flattered herself she could dece), even the brightest of her sex.

In ayeek's time they were on their way to Paris, where it was Miranda's intention to winter. The day they had chosen for the journey proved to be a dull and bitterly cold one, a foretaste of the coming w:nter. They left Victoria by the, eleven o'clock train. They had secured a compartment to themselves, and Miranda, wrapped warmly in lovely akin rugs, was reclining at her ease. The train stopped at Ifenie Hill before it finally started for Dover. It was moving slowly out of the station when, at the last moment, a gentleman rushed up and jumped into the carriage. "I beg your pardon," said he, observing too late that he had entered a reserved compartment. "I would change carriages at once, but I am afraid there is not another stop until we reach Dover." "Oh, do not trouble in the least," said Miranda, lazily, "there is plenty of room for us all."

With this she returned to the novel she was reading, and4the stranger took his seat opposite to Sybil at the further end of the compartment, and drew from his bag newspapers and books. Seeing after a time that Sybil appeared to have nothing to read, he politely offered her a choice of papers. • She took one and thanked him, and they exchanged a few sentences. A little later some trifling. matter led on to a general conversa- tion, in which Miranda joined. The stranger had a pleasant voice, and manner, and was evidently a man of keen observation ainrstrong intellect.' Before they reached Dover Sybil felt as if she had known him quite a long time. His manner was kind without being in the least familiar, and he had a face which would carry him far into the confidence of others. He was tall and rather heavily built, and his movements were somewhat deliberate. As they neared Dover Miranda began to gather together the things she had strewn round the compartment and opened her bag to replace them. In doing this she let fall a letter from her coat pcleket and did not notice that she had done so. Seeing it on the floor, John Thornley—for that was the man's name—picked it Up and. gave it,to her. Though he held the letter but one moment in his hand he, saw the name and address upon it, and also observed the handwriting. He gave it to the owner, watching her carefully whilst he appeared to see nothing. She started slightly and turned pale, then took the letter with an assumed ease of manner; thanking him profusely for go slight a service.

Mr. Tbornley turned away naturally, making some casual remark upon the scenery they were passing at the time. The Channel looked rough, and the ladies, not being good sailers, went below soon as they were on board, and their companie% in the train saw no more of them until they reached Calais. He was glad of this, for he wanted to think out his plans. Curiously enough, it was a case of love at first eight, and, added to this, he found the woman his imagination pictured so Charming surrounded by unusual danger. The letter which he had picked up from the carriage floor had opened his eyes to all this. What should he do? he asked bimself as he paced the deck. How make the girl see the danger he saw.? What reason could she have for believing in him moire than in any man who might happen to cross her path? Yet he felt that something must be done and at once. His blood boiled when he thought of this sweet girl in the hands of a woman whom he knew to be an entirley unscrupulous adventuress. Although he had never actually seen her before he had known of her and her history for •corns time. It was strange enough that he was now on his way to Paris to investigate certain actions of hers with regard to a client of his own. He knew her to be crafty and dishonest. Clever she was without doubt, and was possessed of a certain amount of fascination for some natures. She was a lover of intense gaiety and luxury. She had fooled a number of weak people in, many ways; chiefly, perhaps, in mattErs of finance. Her plan was to always have with her seine innocent and beautiful woman as a decoy to her rece,tiona. She was well known in a certain circle in tari„;. and these people were not unwilling to help her in 'her dishonest practices so long as she made it profitable to themselves. There were times when she had felt the pinch of poverty, when she had risked her last twenty francs upon the gaming table at Monte Carlo and lost; but her wits had, so far, made a way for her, and within a short time she might be seen driving nor neautitui norses in the 1301/1. All this was known to John Thornley ; and when he picked up the envelope addressed in the handwriting of his client he had experienced a shock which lt

large. Mrs. Lister entered just IL I I she was arranging her last bunch of roses. • "Oh, you dear ! " she gushed. "My seem has never looked so beautiful before. You are an artist. It is perfectly glorious." "I thought there were rather too Many flowers," remarked Sybil, timidly. . .
"That i; qUite impossible. The effect is splendid. Now run away and dress, dear, and make yourself as lovely as you have made my rooms."

Sybil slipped on her only evening gown, which, though by no means new, was most becoming to her. it was of a soft black material, and was well moulded to her fine figure. She fastened a delicate spray of flowers across the bodice. Miranda had chosen a gorgeous yellow satin and much jewellery, in which she felt radiant.

The guests b2gtin to arrive. 'They were chiefly French, though a few of them were English. The women were over-dressed and the men affected and bold, or so they seemed to Sybil Hammond's sober taste. Very shortly the card- tables were brought out, and 'Miranda and most of her friends sat down to "Bridge." Sybil refused to play, and, in consequence, found herself left itte-a-t&e with one of the men in whose company she had been the previous day. He impressed her this evening even more unfavourably, if that were possible, than he had done on their first meeting. His look of bold admiration and his outspoken compliment annoyed her beyond measure. She felt very uncom- fortable, and drew a little aside to watch the games. Here another surprise was in store for her. She found money was being paid and received in large sums. Wine was handed round, and after this voices became even louder than before. Mrs. Lister seemed in her element in this scene of extravagance and mirth. Sybil felt distressed, and wished herself back in England. A small clock at her side struck nine, and she suddenly remembered her engagement to see John Thornley. She rose quietly, saying she found the room rather warm. At the door she met a servant bringing her a message. He had arrived and was waiting to see her. She paused a moment in the hall to gain composure, and breathe in a draught of pure air from thc open window, then she quietly entered the small sitting-room into which Mr. Thornley had been shewn. He was struck once more by her beauty as she came towards him. The light fell directly upon her face, which wore at present a look of I reserve and pride. He also thought he saw a look of distress flit across her features. Het, manner was quite calm as she stood before him. "Pardon me this intrusion, Miss Hammond,' he said, almost humbly. "I would not have thrust my presence upon you had not circum- stances required me to do so." "Will you not sit down?" said she, pointing to a chair. She took a seat opposite to him, and waited for him te go on. "You will forgive me whilst I fully explain myself," he said, 'To begin at the beginning, when I stepped into the train at Herne Hill you and Mrs. Listef were complete strangers to me, as far as I knew. If you remember, as we neared Dover I picked up a letter which Mrs. Listo had let fall. For one moment my eyes rested upon the name and address on the envelope, and I experienced a shock, for I at once knew her to , be a woman of doi b`ful reputation. Moreover. I , was on my way to Paris to make some inquiries ' with regard to certain transactions of hers. I have made those inquiries since my arrival, and tlnd that everything my client suspected is correct: Whether he will prosecute her upon my return remains to be seen. She has in a most ingenious' way contrived to possess herself of certain moneys belonging to him. I need not enter' further into detail. You have now sufficient knowledge to act upon. I saw Mrs. Lister's advertisement in the paper, and when recognised her I felt sure that you were behle deceived. I have nothing more to add," he said,l "except that I am here to help you, if it be within my power to do so." Poor Sybil did not know what to say, for she now fully believed in and trusted him, and, she felt ashamed to think of the way in which `she had treated him before.

"I am very sorry," she said, lifting hes beautiful frank eyes to his. "You must bays thought me dreadfully rude and ungrateful when you were trying to do me so great a service. Tc tell the truth, I have been greatly undeceivei since my arrival in Paris. Mrs. Lister and hes friends are not the kind of people with whom could possibly have remained, even if I had noi heard what you have just told me. The questior now is how I am to get away." "If you will take my advice, you will leave al once. May I ask how long you engaged to stay with Mrs. Lister ? "

"We made no definite arrangements. Mrs. Lister said she would try a few weeks and sec how we settled down together." "I leave for London at eight o'clock to- morrow morning. Would it be asking too much trust in a stranger if I were to say how delighted I should be to escort you back to England? forget though, you hardly even know my name. I am John Thornley, junior partner in the firm of Thornley and Wallace, Solicitors, Lincoln's Inn. You may possibly have heard the name." It was an old-established firm, and Sybil remembered to have seen it mentioned in thc papers. "I will be ready fo- that train in the morning," she said, decidedly, " nd I will travel with you if you are quite sure I shall not be troubling you in any way. You hav been most kind, and I am very grateful." "Oh. ple Ise do not m.,ntion it," he ssid, rising to lerve. "Then Twill Is here with acrb at 7.15.

- Sybil r-Murned to th ro tn hre r,ambl:ng was going on a-st, c. She tlicuglit toe e ning muld never end, but at length, the lust g :est having departe4 Miranda and Oil w(n left alone. Then followed a scene. Sybil told Miranda that she found it.impossible to stay any longer with her, and asked to be allowed to return to England at once. Whereupon Mir .ud% became greatly enraged, and heaped rep.da hes upon the girl, for what she was pleased to call her prudish fancy. Finally, she marched out of the room saying: "I shall not allow you to leave me until at least three months have elapsed." Sybil retired to her own room, drew out her trunks and carefully packed all her belongings. She then lay down upon her bed and tried to sleep. She was restless, and afraid of sleeping too long. However, she was up and dressed in very good time, and had soon made her flue! preparations.. Presently she saw a cab draw up to the house. She opened her door quietly, dese^ndcd the stairs, and asked the omseierge to go and carry down her boxes, and to make no noise about it, as Mariam° was sleeping. No one was astir in the fiat, the servants being later than usual th morning. She i eturned to her room, took u her rug and small handbag, shut the door as g ntly :Is possible, walked quietly down- stairs, gave scm me my to the con erge, and stepped into the cab, followed by John Thorniey. She had counted every franc of her money, and was much reli, v.-A to find that ale possessed plenty for the return journey. How thvnkful she wee not to be obliged to borrow from her new- found friend!

It was a bag day's :ourney before they reached her country 1 o no, but the hours slipped away so pleasantly. John Tho:nley was most kind add thoughtful in every woy of Sybil's comfort, and congratulated her warmly upon the spirit she had shewn through the whole affair. He insisted upon seeing her to her father's house, and giving to him his own account of the episode. Mr. Hammond was most grateful to him for the part he had played, and thanked him again and again. This proved to be Sybil's only attempt at earning her own living as a companion. Within six months' time she became the dearly-loved wife of John Thornley. As for Miranda, after the receipt of a letter from England, she thought it wiser to change her plans for the wine , so she moved into Spain under another name, i nd has not been seen either in Paris or London sin e Sybil's return.

div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
THE HARROGATE CONVENTION.

The chief event among the Free ‘Chnrches during the past month has been the National Convention for the Deepening of Spiritual Life held at Harrogate. This was the first of what is intended to be an annual institution—in fact, a sort of Free Church Keswick. The Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., who was in charge of the gather - lugs, is a well-known leader of the Keswick. movement, besides being connected with 'reli- gious Conventions under di rent auspices throughout the entire. world. Mr. Meyer had seen that at Keswick the Anglican element pre- dominated, and that the Free Cinzches were in need of the spiritual, teaching which charac- terises Keswick. Other leaders among the Free Churches eon rred in his .i.. aof estaolishing a Convention, to emi..hasise Keswick teachings to the Free C:iur hes by Free Church leaders; and consequentlytile National Council o:ga:dsed the meetings at .Harrogate. . .
INTEII2i:TING rnoGnAmmr..

The programme followed at these meetinga was decidedly an interesting one, deparing somewhat from the usual order of meetin,';;.s. At 7.30 in the morning the members attended for a Sunrise Prayer Meeting. This was quii,e different to ordinary Prayer Meetings,, M. Meyer insisting on the petitions being short and to the. point, and those present say that it was often the most impressive and enjoyable feature a the whole day. At 11 ()Clock each morning a great .Devotional Session was held, at which leaders such as Dr. Horton, Dr. Bendel Harris, Rev. H. Elvet Lewis, M.A., and Gipsy Smith took part. Instead of there being a meeting in the afternoon the time was given up to a ramble; the Over-tea Conference at o o'clock was always a deeply interesting. proceeding>. Mr. Meyer catechised some of the leaders each day as to various forms of Christian service, with the most excellent results. In the evening great Evangelistic Services were held, conducted by Gipsy Smith, who was supported by Mr. Herbert Booth, ion of General Booth.

div.head: DR. HORTON AND FOREIGN MISSION WORK.
div.p: DR. HORTON AND FOREIGN MISSION WORK.

Something like a sensation was caused at one of the Over-tea Conferences by some statements by Dr. Horton, and these have given rise to a certain amount of misunderstanding and criti- cism. Dr. Horton spoke most glowingly of the good work accomplished in the Mission Meld. Some of the good work there to-day, he said, was much finer than anything recorded in the works of the Acts of the Apostles. There was nothing nobler in the first ages of the Christian Church than the way the Chinese had died rather than renounce Christ. It was a story to wake their hearts melt. Mr. Meyer asked if the Missionary cause was advancing, and Dr. Horton at once replied, "You are making next to no headway. By an extraordinary mathe- matical arrangement God only allows you to win the heathen world in proportion to the interest of the Church." It was not a question of numbers. There were enough missionaries on the field to convert the world, but they were not backed up by the Church at home. These statements have been interpreted since to show that Dr. Horton was unduly pessimistic, but, of course, this is the reverse of the case. Dr. Horton was speaking from the widest stand- point, and* his remarks should not be read to mean that the splendid organisations of the Christian Church in the Foreign Field are making no progress. At the same time when one realises the tremendous extent of the heathen population, the millions of China and the large proportion of the world's population still embraced in the Moslem faith, it is difficult to deny that we are making next to no head- way. There is room for a great deal more interest_ in Foreign Mission Work on the part nf the 'Churches, and Dr. Hortores words ought to arouse considerable heart-searching amongst those who have .not hitherto supported the cause of Foreign Missions.

div.head: GIPSY SMITH'S CROSS-EXAMINATION.
div.p: GIPSY SMITH'S CROSS-EXAMINATION.

This month's Free Church Chronicle has a long account of the Harrogate meetings, in- cluding a description of a remarkable service in which Gipsy Smith was publicly cross- examined on "The Way of Salvation by Mr. Meyer. "

div.head: EDUCATION STRUGGLE.
div.p: THE EDUCATION STRUGGLE.

The House of Lords has read the Education Bill a second time, and without a division, and now both Houses are on holiday, and the struggle will not be resumed until October 23rd. Thus we have a lull in the strife, and time to look around and prepare. It is perhaps notable that the tone of the speeches in the Upper Chamber was studiously moderate, though the threats of vital amendment were many. What will be done in the autumn no one can say, but it must be acknowledged that the position of affairs has been considerably altered by the decision of the Court of Appeal in the West Riding of Yorkshire case. This decision should immensely help the Government 'in its dealing with the Upper Chamber. In some quarters it is prebumed with too much alacrity that the battle is over. This is expecting too much from the good sense and popular feeling of the House of Lords.

div.head: FREE CHURCH POSITION.
div.p: FREE CHURCH POSITION.

The position of Free Churchmen is quite clear in the matter. They have welcomed the Edu- cation Bill as an honest attempt to settle a vexed question in a just and equitable manner. To Mr. Birrell, especially, they have felt grateful for the statesmanlike way in which he intro- duced and has carried through the measure. At the same time it would be idle to deny the strong feeling of the Free Churches that the Government has gone as far as it possibly can go in the way of concessions.

div.head: NO COMPROMISE.
div.p: NO COMPROMISE.

Clause 4, for instance, has been viewed all along with grave dislike on the part of members of the Free Churches. It is perfectly certain that any attempt to make serious concessions would mean that Nonconformity throughout the entire country would be against accepting them. The Free Churches could never accept the alterations in the measure outlined by the Primate, the Duke of Devonshire, and others during the debate in the House of Lords. The National Free Church Council is keenly alive to the situation, and there is every probability that, should the House of Lords carry out the threat of vital amendment, the National Council itself will be specially summoned and the united action of the Free Churches determined by representatives from the entire country. The feeling of the Free Churches is that the limit of concessions has been reached, and that there must be no further compromise.

div.head: CHRISTIAN IN PUBLIC LIFE.
div.p: THE CHRISTIAN IN PUBLIC LIFE.

Dr. Horton contributes a striking article to this month's Free Churchman on "The Christian and Public Life," in which he insists in the followers of Christ taking their share in the public life of the world. "Men do not seem to see, he says, "that if Christ is the real Saviour of the world He wants a voice in every licensing law; He must have His will carried out in such a carnal matter as the sale of strong drink, and He requires His servants to do it because one cannot depend on any people to • carry out a simple principle of disinterested righteousness except those men in whom He dwells. We need to be saved from a position of indifference and apathy and selfishness and personal absorp- tion which allows us to see a great community ruined for want of the simplest elements of government and administration."

div.head: GERMAN GIPSIES AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE GERMAN GIPSIES AT ST. HELENS.

_ The second band of German gipsies just now travelling this part of the country. passed through Prescot and St. Helens on Tuesday night. They were met at Eccleston Hill by a large body of police, and kept on the move until the borough boundary had been cleared at Haydock.

AWONDERFUL DISCOVERY.—This is the age of research and exoerlment, when all nature, so to speak, is ransacked by the scientific for the comfort and happiness of man. Science has indeed made giant strides during the past Century, and among the —by no means least important—discoveries in medicine comes that of THHIZAPION

This preparation is unquestionably one of the most genuine and reliable Patent Medicines ever introduced, and nas we understand, been used in the Continental Hospitals by Ricord, Rostan, Tobert. Veipeau, Malsonnenve the well- known Chassaignac, and indeed by all who are regarded as authorities in such matters, including the celebrated Lallemand, and Dux, by whom it was some time since uniformly adopted,and that It is worthy the attention of those who require such a remedy we think there is no doubt. From the time of Aristotle downwards a potent agent in the removal of these diseases has (like Ihe famed philosopher's stone) been the object of search of some hopeful generous minds ; and far beyond the mere power—if such could ever have been discovered—of transmuting the baser metals into gold is surely the discovery of a remedy so potent as to re- plenish the falling energies In the one case, and in the other so effectually, speedily and safely to expel from the system the poisons of acquired or Inherited disease In all their potent forms as to leave no taint or trace behind. Such is the new French Remedy THICRAPI,ON, which may certainly rank with, If not take precedence of, many of the discoveries of our day, about which no !little ostentation and noise hays been made, and the extensive and ever-Increasing demand that has been created for this medicine wherever introduced appears to prove that it is destined to east into oblivion all those questionable remedies that were formerly the sole reliance of medical men.
