REPORTS from all parts of THE WEST the kingdom show that RIDING JUDG- local education authorities 3IENT. are very much perturbed by the judgment of the Court

of Appeal in the West- Riding Schools case. Coming as it did in Bank Holiday week, when all the authorities were in vacation,the judgment has not, up to the present, been generally considered by them. Now that the vacations are nearly over and authorities are beginning to meet again it is evident that the'effects are going to be a great deal more far-reaching than was at first thought prob- able. It is true that the judgment itself does not prohibit local authorities from paying for denom- inational teaching ; it only says they need not do so, that payment for such teaching is not necessary to " maintain and keep efficient " a non- provided school. But a careful perusal of the terms of the judgment has shown the expert I advisers of local authorities that there is more than a probability that if the further question were put to the Courts, that is, whether a local authority may pay for denominational teaching, the Courts would decide that by paying , for such instruction authorities are acting ultra vires. No wonder thou that even authorities containing a majority of the friends of Voluntary schools are hesitating to continue such payments. The possibility, nay the probability, is that on a ques- tion such as this some ratepayer will in every district appear before the district auditor of the Local Government Board and take objections to payments made by the authority for the mainten- ance of denominational instruction. The auditor may decide, in the light of the judgment, that there is no authority in the Education Acts for such payments, and, if so, he must surcharge the members of the local authority. It is hardly likely that men who give their time and ability to the public service will be prepared to take the addi- tional risk.

So far, indeed, as actual dacisionc of local education authorities have been arrived at they shew that payments for denominational teaching will pretty generally be discontinued. The point then arises—will the managers be prepared to make up the difference to the teachers, or will they allow the teachers to work at the lower salary F We gather from a letter in the " Times " 'by the BISHOP OF MANCHESTER that managers will let the teachers suffer. He takes it that managers will " hand over to the teachers all that they receive from the local authorities, and the teachers will revert to the position, or 'something like • the position, in which they were in respect of salaries before 1901" Of course, he is sorry for them, but having expressed his sympathy he passes by on the other side. One sentence, however, in the Bisuop's letter should shew those who believe in full public con- trol and no religious tests for teachers that, vain. able as is the judgment of the Court of Appeal, it does not give us anything like a satisfactory solution of the Education problem. "Meanwhile," says Dr. lirtox, "we retain the entire ownership

of our schools, and the right of appointing teachers, which is the key of the position, so far as religious instruction is concerned; and our denominational teaching is a matter of right and dot of favour." In other words, so long as the appointment of the teachers rests with them, he does not mind much. Tests can be applied, and it can be made a condition of appointment that the teacher shall give denominational instruction. But the poor teacher will only receive as salary the amount of money received from the local authority, which may not, and most likely will not,inelude any pay- ment for religious teaching. If any justification were needed for proceeding with the present Education Bill it is surely to be found in this episcopal deliverance. Liberal policy consists of three fundamental propositions: first, full public control; secondly, no religious tests for teachers; and, thirdly, no denominational teaching at the public expense. The West Riding judgment deals only with the third of these, and does not ex- plicitly give all that is required even there. Mr. BIRRELL'S Bill gives us all three, and nothing short of its provisions should be accepted as a final solution of the matter.

Si r Henry Campbell- THE PREMIER'S Bannerman's first Session SORROW. as Prime Minister has been clouded by a great domestic sorrow. During the whole of the year the health of his wife has been such as to cause him the greatest anxiety, and it is not too much to say that the whole nation has watched with sympa- thetic concern his devotion to the partner of ~ 4 his joys and sorrows. It was with the sincerest ' pleasure that the news was received that her Ladyship was sufficiently recovered to make the journey to Marienbad, but now unhappily, comes the announc,ment of a fatal termination to her illness. The Prime Minister's misfortune will be sincerely regretted by men of all parties in politics, for, despite the keenness of Parliamentary struggles, one characteristic of British public life is that party feeling never extinguishes human sympathy and anxiety for the private sorrows even of a political apponent. Lady Campbell-Bannerman was not herself well known to the public. They only knew her as the woman who for forty-six years had shared the domestic life and ministered to the material comfort of the most popular ()rime Minister of modern times. All of us, whether we share or distrust the views of Sir Henry, sympa- thise with him in his misfortune. Sir Henry has had to pass through many storms, and now that he has come into his own it seems hard that his triumph should be over-clouded by this great domestic sorrow. The private lives of public men become in many cases more or less public property. That has hardly been the case with the Prime Minister. Long and strenuous as his public career has been, he has always shewn that he wished his privat3 life to be really private. But at a time like this we can surely, alongside our admiration for the man's public career and work, express our sympathy with him and pay a tribute to the devotion and self-affacement of the lady who, since the Premier was only 22 years old, had been his life's helpmeet.

, Not very long ago, we were VOTES FOR WO3IEIN. taken to task by a corres- pondent for our criticism of 4e" savage suffragettes" and their conduct in besieging Mr. Asquith and refusing to keep the peace. While maintaining our attitude in refer- ence to this matter we had some difficulty in making clear the fact that we heartily sympathised with the cause which the suffragettes had at heart. It was their methods only we deplored, as we always shall when they go to the lengths which they did prior to the imprison- ment of Miss Kenney and two of her surporters. Agitation is doubtless necessary, lan there is a marked difference between conduccing an agitation and creating a disturbance. La° night we took the opportunity of hearing g'ss Pankhurst at Bridge Foot, and our regret at the absence of that fiery little mill girl, Miss Kenney, was common to the large crowd. With regard co Miss Pankhurst we have nothing hut what is i complimentary to say. She spoke logically, n- cisively, and with unmistakable enthusiasm for her cause. If ever anyone was fighting an uphill fight it is this talented young lady and her friends, and they fight not with the courage of despair but with the courage born of a high and confident hope. Miss Pankhurst is sure of ulti- mate success, and we trust that success will early crown her efforts, though we do not go all the way with her in wishing women to have precisely the same voting rights as men. Miss Pank- hurst gets considerably in advance of her time in demanding so much. Responsible women— householders, and others with a sense of citizen- ship created by experience and knoWledge—should be entitled to exercise the franchise, but that the average young woman of to-day should have a vote is asking rather too much. She may fairly claim the right of representation by members of her sex,but she must needs show herself capable of understanding national and political issues before she has the privilege of voting upon them. Miss Pankhurst is one in ten thousand, and when there are more like her it will be time to think of granting them the franchise on attaining woman- hood's estate. Manhood suffrage will have to come first,and womanhood suffrage some distance after. Meanwhile, God-speed to the "votes for women crusade so long as it follows the line of fair agita- tion and propagandism.

It was the custom for the professional and other habitues of the Warrington Police Court to often allude to the late Mr. EI. Taylor as the" bishop.'' The title may not have had much in the way of suitability to recommend it but it stuck to the Police Court Missionary for years, and was always applied in a kindly spirit. Mr. Taylor was oile of those men whom it was impossible to imagine having an enemy in the wide world. He spent his lifetime doing good, and the man who could or would have quarrelled with him must have been, a queerly constituted being, The " bishop" breathed kindliness in all he said, and unselfishness was the keynote of his actions. For fifteen years he minis- tered at the Warrington Police Court, rendering aid and advice to the outcast and the fallen. Rarely was he absent, and frequently were his valued ministrations sought by the magistrates on behalf of some unfortunate being who occupied the prisoners' dock. There was plenty of scope for a man like Mr. Taylor, and he gloried in his none too savoury work. Every cause which had for its aim the uplifting of the fallen, was assured of his active sympathy, and his kindly voice will be missed in many and strange quarters. The nature of his end was tragically sudden, but he died practicallylin harness and leaves behind him the record of work well done, and memories of a wholly admirable personality. .

When the Beautiful War. THE CHILDREN AND rington movement we ° THE BEAUTIFUL. lanched, the promoters di. wisely in deciding to make bold effort to enlist the co-operation of the children. Everyone felt that unless the children were won, over to the cause of beautification, not much pro 7 gress could be made. Townspeople who have gardens and take a pride in them spoke feelingli of the depredations of youngsters who seemed to consider it their peculiar right to seize choice blooms immediately they appeared and t° committ various wanton acts of destruction. We do not say that the Beautiful Warrington Society has succeeded in stopp;ng all this— would be too much to expect—but undoubtedly e great deal has been done to instil into the minds of the young a love of the beautiful. There is nothing more calculated to attain this end than to give the juveniles a personal interest in the scheme. The Society could not have hit upon a happier idea than to distribute 2,500 plants to the scholars at the day schools and offer prizes for their cultivation.

WOOD, Piano Dealer and Tuner, 47, Old London-road., Stockton Heath.—Advt. Wedding.—Rice —Hall. A wedding of considerable local interest was solemnized at the Baptist Church, Golborne-street, on Thursday afternoon, when the contracting parties were Mr. George Frederick Patrick Rice, of the Borough Treasurer's office, . son of Sergeant-Major Rice, Thynne-street, and Lilian Martha Hall, daughter of Mr. Joseph Hall, Causeway-avenue. There was a large attendance at the Church to witness the ceremony, which was performed by the Rev. J. F. Matthews. The bride was attired in a dress of white silk and Brussels net, with a veil surmounted by a wreath of orange blossom: Her ornament was a gold curb bracelet the gift of the bridegroom, and she carried a beauti- ful shower bouquet of white lilies. The bridesmaids were Miss Clara Davenport, Miss Susie Rice and Miss Adeline Rice. The first named was attired ic a dress of pale blue silk with hat to match and carried a bouquet of red roses. Miss Susie Rice wore a dress of pink silk and a pink silk hat and carried a bouquet similar to that of Miss Davenport, while Miss Adeline Rice wore a dress of white silk and carried a bouquet of mysanthemums. The bridesmaids ornaments were Miss Davenport and Miss Rice, gold signet rings set with pearls, and Miss Adeline Rice, a gold brooch set with pearls, gifts of the bridegroom. Corporal Rice, of the Army Service Corps, was the ' best man. Mr. Clatworthy presided at the organ arid rendered a number of appropriate selections. The wedding breakfast was held in the Golborne-street schoolroom, after which the happy couple left for , Llandudno where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride travelled in a wine coloured costume with a cream lace hat to match. UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS. Advt.— Concert at the Cricket Pavilion. The Warrington Cricket Club's pavilion at Arpley presented a pleasing appearance on Saturday evening when a highly successful concert was held. Chinese lanterns and plants had been utilized for the decora- tion of the building and the effect produced was very picturesque. An admirable programme had been arranged and there was a large gathering of members and friends. Miss Marie Houghton's beautiful soprano voice found full scope in "A spring morning" and " The nightingale " which she gave in a most tasteful manner. Miss -Fairhurst (contralto) delighted the audi- ence with a feeling interpretation of " Come back to me," Miss Houghton and Messrs. J. Rabbitt and J. W. Bibby assisting in the chorus with effect. Later Miss Fairhurst sang" Kathleen Mavourneen"which gave so much pleasure that an encore was accorded. Mr. Rabbitt was in excellent voice and fully maintained his reputation with the charming eongs " My dreams" and " English rose." Mr. J. W. Bibby elicited warm applause for his creditable rendering of" A soldier's song " and Mn. Peter Bate was heard to distinct advantage in " Song of the Toreador" and "A. life that lives for you." Responding to an encore for the latter he gave the stirring " Veteran's. song " with great success. The quartettes " Strange adventure " ("Yeomen of the Guard ") and " Brightly dawns our Wedding Day (" Mikado ") were artistically given by Misses Houghton and Fairhurst and Messrs. Rabbitt and Bibby, the voices blending splendidly. The instrumental trios "Colombe " and " Gipsy Rondo " by Messrs. R. H. Pearson (violin), Henry Bond (cello) and W. H. Payton (piano) were skilfully played, and proved an acceptable feature. The humorous part of the programme was in the capable hands of Mr. Alf Grounds, who created great merriment with his songs and sketches. Mr. W. H. Payton, lafus. Bac., ably discharged the duties of •accompanist.

The patriots are congratu MUSIC AND lilting themselves that the PATRIOTISM. forthcoming musical festive- at Birmingham is to be dis- tinguished by an attention to the works of British zomposers, which is not usual in these gatherings. The principal work to be performed is Sir Edward ?Agar's " The Apostles " which will be followed by " The Kingdom," his latest work, to be heard for the first time. In addition to that there will be compositions from other native musicians, so that the procession of names on the programme Will not be wholly unpronounceable—a blessing for which, no doubt, some portion of the audiences Will be thankful. Possibly in this concession to national sentiment there may be the force of a movement which will accomplish even greater 'things later on. But those who are always crying it for patronage for British composers should vs a lesson from Dr. Elva. If the prejudice ,ainst British works which is alleged to exist wore actually a fact, Sir Edward would have had a poor chance. As it is, his recognition in England has been very complete. The truth of the matter is that a succession of mediocre work has had the effect of making musicians chary of accepting com- positions of untried value. No English composer who is really great or who is even beyond the usual ruck will go unacknowledged.

* * What is termed the "No-hat craze" has more devotees than ever this summer, and it is heartily to be welcomed from the health standpoint. Nature provided us all with a natural thatch which can be made to suffice for head-covering in most weathers. Probably there would be less premature baldness if the past generation had been brought up with a disregard for any head-covering but the natural one. There are some curious results of this harking back to the pre-hat days. More than one clergy-man has expressed strong disapproval of ladies coming hatless to church. Only on Sunday last a lady was requested to leave the Menai Bridge Church for this reason. The clerical mind seems to see something immodest or irreverent in the head of a girl adorned only by her hair., Yet it is an unwritten law—" hats off in church "—as regards men which none of them would think of breaking. Why this difference as regards the head-gear of the sexes at public worship? It seems to us merely silly, and there is no doubt that if all ladies went hatless to church the preacher would get more undivided attention than he does at present.

The question is being IS THERE A CRUSOE'S discussed as to whether ISLE? Juan Fernandez, which, we are informed by cable, has disappeared during the seismic disturbances in South America, is the real Robinson Crusoe's island. This is certainly the island on which Alexander Selkirk, the unfortunate Scottish sailor Spent five solitary years, and a monument to him was erected there nearly forty years ago by the. Germans who then colonised it. Thera can be no doubt that the story which Defoe heard ,born the lips of Selkirk influenced him very *lnch when he came to write "Robinson Crusoe," but the fact remains that he made ,the island on which his hero was wrecked one of *the West Indian group. He distinctly tells us it %Was in the neighbourhood of the Carribbeans, and not far from the mouth of the Orinoco. That being the case, even if the report of its disappear- ance be true, the loss of Juan Fernandez will not be so great a blow to sentiment. Probably there tlever was any particular island which had the'right to be called Crusoe's Isle, its existence being really confined to the novelist's imagination. It is ,true that a number of recluses, before and since Selkirk's day, have from time to time lived on Juan Fernandez. Indeed, its name is taken from the first of them, a Spanish sailor, who lived in Voluntary exile there for several years. There are teeny islands in various parts of the world on Vhich lonely exiles have lived, and which would Ine equally ideal spots for anyone who wished to ce a modern ,Crusoe.

Gloucester's victory over THE INWARDNESS Yorkshire associates in the OF THE Championship problem two CHAMPIONSHIP. counties which, for one cause at any rate, not only the cricket world but the whole world of sport rejoices to see bracketed in the supreme rivalry. Yorkshire and Kent have both set their faces against the importation of Colonial cricketers, and have insisted that the talent on which county cricket is based shall be native found. This is the true n sportsmanlike position, and there is not a the ,rtBn3so in the land who will not welcome t - new justification which the contest has given ‘ 0 these eminently sound principles. Both teams s!and in the forefront of British cricket. I‘.ent has her nurseries for young cricketers, While Yorkshire declines to nlay a man who is 1. waged, Yorkshire-born. Trott, Roche,Vogler,Kermodef L. 0. S. Poidevin, and C. A. Olivierre may ..be excellent cricketers, and something may be due to ;the Empire, since Australia, the West Indies, and -outh Africa conspired to produce tli.m, but ;they are not home-made goods. Sport knows no freedom of trade. In fact, there should be no ,trade in sport at all. "Art and sport for their ,bu'n sakes" is a good working principle. Let the Championship go as it may, one fight in English :saPort has been well wad, and that is the contest between English talent or a reasonable qualifying Iterm and that unbridled professionalism which ,Vould make English cricket an exotic plant like lorchids, to be commanded only by long purses.

div.head: PREMIER BEREAVED.
div.p: THE PREMIER BEREAVED.
Lady Campbell-Bannerman Passes Quietly Away.
THE KING'S AUTOGRAPH MESSAGE OF SYMPATHY.

Lady Campbell-Bannerman died at Marienbad at five o'clock on Thursday afternoon. Her ladyship (says Renter's correspondent), passed away quietly in her sleep without any struggle. Inhalations oi oxygen were resorted to during the last two hods.

The immediate cause of death was exhaustion, her ladyship having been unable to take nourishment for the last three days. Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman , and Dr. Ott were present at the bedside. The illness of Lady Campbell-Bannerman was of long-standing, and it is a melancholy fact that since the Premier relinquished his town house in Belgrave- square in the early part of the present year, in order to take over his official residence, her ladyship has only left the house upon two occasions—once for the purpose of staying at Dover, and again, at the close of last session, to spend the summer vacation at Marien- bad.

On the latter occasion the family medical man travelled with the party-, and during the three weeks or so which have been spent abroad Dr. Ott, the famous specialist,-las been in constant attendance. The journey to Marienbad was made in easy stages, and at the close herladyship was stated to have borne it as well as could be expected. A few- days ago, however, a serious relapse took place.. Throughout her long illness, and uPon the several occasions when her condition has been critical, the King has been a constant inquirer. As soon as King Edward heard of the death of Lady Campbell-Bannerman his Majesty sent an autograph letter to the Premier by Sir Stanley Clarke, expressing deepest sympathy. The sad news spread rapidly through Marienbad, and warm sympathy was expressed on all sides with the Premier.

DRINK AND BRUTALITY AT RUNCORN At Runcorn on Tuesday, Thomas Inman, a powerful- looking young man, an ex-marine infantryman, was brought up on a warrant charged with using threats to his father, John Inman, of 5, Speakman-street. The prisoner pleaded guilty.—The father said the prisoner came home on Saturday afternoon and threw the tea things all over the place. At night he locked the house up, and told his family not to allow the prisoner in. The prisoner smashed the windows and burst open the door, and attacked his father, whore he clutched by the throat and threatened to murder. He was pulled off by his.half-brother, Abraham Lunt, and several neighbours. The prisoner was in drink, but not drunk. He had been on the snree for a long time, and had done no work for ten weeks. Witness said he had begged of him on his knees to give up drinking, but he said he had his own road to go and he should go it.—The prisoner, who had nothing to say, was sentenced to twenty-one days' hard labour in default of finding sureties to keep the peace.

RAILWAY PRESENTATION AT ST. HELENS. An interesting presentation took place on Monday night at the St. Helens station of the London and North-Western Railway Company,when Mr. Whistlecroft the stationmaster, presented a massive marble clock to Mr. William Richarclson,one of the parcel porters on the 'occasion of his marriage. Mr. Richardson has been on the St. Helens staff nearly twenty years, and is most highly respected by everyone connected with the station -

THE TRADESMAN'S TRAP. INLAND REVENUE PROSECUTION AT ST. HELENS. , Another charge against a tradesman of keeping a "carriage " without a licence was heard at St. Helens on Monday, when Charles Shell, of 189, Greentleld-road, was summoned by Harold A. Pickles.—Mr. Leghorn prosecuted, and said that on March 19, the trap was used by a Mr. and Mrs. Clark for a pleasure trip.—Mr. Pickles admitted that the defendant told him they had it out merely for trying the horse which Mr. Clark thought of purchasing.—Mr. Fox, for the defence, in addressing the court, said that this summons was surely nothing but irritation. It was trying to annoy other- wise honest citizens by bringing them before the court on the most paltry and the most trivial cases that mind could conceive.— ('he defenthnt gave evidence that he only used the trap for carrying out the goods which were ordered. He never used it to solicit orders.—The Chairman (Mr. Sharpies) said the bench was advised that the case did not come within the exceptions pro- vided for, and the defendant would be 9ned -s. 6d. and 12s. costs.

_ ATTEMPTED SUICIDES AT ST. HELENS. At St. Helens police Court on Saturday the two cases of attempted suicide which were reported last week were again brought before Mr. J. B. Leach and Alder- man Green.—Bridget Manniort, the wife, of a rag- gatherer, who tried to hang herself, said she was very sorry, and that she had taken the pledge and intended to keep it at least for twelve months. She blamed her husband, but he had also taken the pledge, and she would never do anything of the kind- again.- -On this promise she was discharged.—l Matthew Black- more, a collier, of 6, Tickle-street, S. Helens, was also charged with attempted suicide by taking laudanum.— Sergeant Ackers met the man in Liverpool-road at eloven o'clock on Friday night, the 17th inst., and he told the sergeant he had been taking laudanum, and that he wanted to cut the thread of life as he was tired of living.—Chief Inspector Goodall said that the man's sister had told him that a month before Blackmore went to her house and said he had taken some laudanum, but it had not taken effect. He was very much upset about being out of work.—The magistrates asked if the man had been examined by a doctor, but, as there was no information to this effect, prisoner was remanded for another week, notwithstanding his entreaties to be allowed to go.

ALARMING COLLIERY MISHAP. SIXTEEN MEN IN PERIL. An alarming pit-shaft accident occurred at the Bold Colliery on Saturday morning. It appears that about a 1 quarter to six o'clock, when sixteen men were being sent down the shaft, and another sixteen were being raised, the engine went some distance beyond the usual stopping-place, with the result that the men in the cage coming up were "hung up " in the headgear, and the sixteen men who were descending were thrown with 'terrible force on to the landing at the bottom. The men up alof escaped with nothing more than a fright and ' a shake ; but two of the men in the cage down at the bottom of the shaft were sightly injured. They were all thrown at the top and bottom decks of the cage, and John Moran, thirty-eight, of 214, Reginald-road,and John Deans, of 57,Houghton-road,were injured about the legs. After some delay they were raised to the ti.rface, and the two injured men were taken to Dr. Casey's surgery, and attended to, after which they were taken home. Tee accident occurred in the shaft where five men were killed and thirteen injured on January 10th, 1905. For some time considerable apprehension was caused owing to the statement that all the siKteen men had been killed. Most of the men reside in the neighbour- hood of St. Helens Junction, but fortunately the fears of the people of the district were allayed when it was found that all of them had luckily escaped with eight injuries. At about seven o'clock, as coiled wire was being loaded up near the entrance to the works the " stack" from which the wire was being taken tilted over and fell ncon Martin Sweeney, aged 22, labourer in the wire mill„ a single man living in lodgings at 6, Leicester-street. There was an interesting gathering at the Railway and Commercial Hotel, Widnes, on Wednesday even- ing, when journalists of Widnes and Warrington met to present Mr. Frank Fennelly, manager of the "Runcorn Guardian," with a token of their esteem and good wishes on the occasion of his marriage. The gift took the form of a handsome writing desk, suitably inscribed. Mr. Joseph Archer presided, and referred in terms of the highest praise to Mr. Fenuelly's good qualities, and to his interest in all that appertained to the advancement of the profession. —Mr. Henry Isherwood, of Warrington, made the presentation and on behalf of the journalist's of the district wished Mr. and Mrs. Fennelly a long and happy married life. These sentiments were heartily endorsed by all present. Mr. Fennelly responded in an inter- esting speech, full of reminiscences, and said he would always treasure the present as a mark of friendship. He sincerely thanked the subscribers and expressed the hope that the happy relations which existed between local Preissmen would long continue. ! _ !

PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST I BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Rescue at Sankey Bridges A gallant rescue from droaning was witnessed at Sankey Bridges on Wednesday evening. It appears that about 5.30 a boy named Molyneux, aged about twelve, and living in the neighbourhood, was playing on the hanks, of the St. Helens and Sankey Canal when he -overbaldbced and fell into the deep part. A number of people made efforts to reach him but they were unavailing. Fortunately, Mr. John Rose, head of the caustic department at Messrs. Crosfield's works and who is also first officer of the Crosfield division of the St. John Ambulance Brigade, arrived upon the scene and, divesting himself of his hat and coat, immediately plunged in to the rescue. The boy had sunk once but Mr., Rose succeeded in bringing him to the side. The Silvester method of resuscitation was applied for several minutes and consciousness was restored. Afterwards the boy was taken to the house of Mr. Dale in Hood lane and supplied with dry clothes. He was soon able to go home, little the worse for his immersion. It is worthy of note that this is the second time that Mr. Rose has saved a person from drowning and in the first case artificial respiration had to be resorted to for half an hour. His conduct is certainly worthy of recognition and should be brought before the notice of the Royal Humane Society.

HAYDOCE COLLIER'S FATAL ACCIDENT. Hugh Topping, a young Haydock man, who was employed at the old Boston Pit, belonging to lessr.s. Evans and Co., died in the Haydock Cottage Hospital on Sunday. Topping was working down the the pit shaft about a fortnight ago, when he was struck on the left elbow by the descending cage. The arm was shattered, and had to be amputated, but the poor fellow never recovered from the shock. ACCIDENT AT NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS FLOWER

div.head: SHOW.
div.p: SHOW.

The annual exhibition of plants, flowers, and vege- tables, was held on Saturday, at Newton-le-Willows, but for the second time in succession the local society have experienced the misfortune of having their efforts spoiled by the blowing down of the marquee. The gale which sprang up during the night blew broadside on the tent,which,however,withstood the elements well. But about eight o'clock a spar connecting the uprights gave I way. This was made good as well as possible, but about half-past nine a sudden gust caught the canvas near the middle and carried all before it. All the stakes were drawn on one side, and the great sheet of canvas was down except at one end. There would be sixty or seventy people in at the time putting the finishing touches to the exhibits. Tables were overturned, plants crushed into a valueless heap, vegetables, fruit, broken plates and boxes were hurled allover the place, men and women could be seen scrambling through the debris, escaping from the flap- ping sheets. One woman was rescued in a fainting con- dition. But in spite of the unusual violence with which the place collapsed there was not a single case of injury, though escapes were numerous. What stuff was fit for showing was afterwards spread out on the grass and there judged. EARLESTOWN TRADES DISPUTE.

The drillers numbering between seventy and eighty, employed at the Vulcan Foundry, Earlestown, are still out, having failed to put in an appearance on Monday morning. The men last week applied for an advance of 3s. a week, and, as they were informed by Mr. Richards, the works manager, that each man must make a personal application to his shop foreman, the reply appears to have been misunderstood. They declined to work over- time, and were consequently suspended for a couple of days. They were informed that the firm would keep their places open until Saturday. On Friday night the men held a meeting, when some of them expressed the opinion that there had been a misunderstanding. It is to be borne in mind that the drillers are recruited from the general labourers, and some have only been working on a machine for a few weeks, and the firm wish to treat each case on its merits. The men on Saturday refused to go in,but had no alternative proposition to make. The works manager informed them that he could not guarantee keeping open the men's places, but it is understood that the firm desires to treat the matter in a conciliatory spirit, and it only needs a little exercise of diplomacy to bring the matter to a satisfactory issue.

div.p: HAYDOCK JURYMAN'S CWIPLAINT.

At a colliery inquest held by Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, at the Waggon Hotel, Haydock, on Wednesday, a juryman made a stroll,' complaint as to the way in I which he had been treated at the Cottage Hospital on ' the previous day.—Mr. Abbott (the juryman) said , that when he was summoned on an inquest he always took it that he was the servant of the coroner, and I bound to obey his orders. Soon after he was summoned as a jurymaa he went to the hospital mortuary in the I usual way to view the body of Hugh Topping, but he I was distinctly told he was not to see the body. He I waited ten minutes, and then had to go away. I —The Coroner : Who told you to go.—Mr. Abbott : A young man who went to ask the nurse for the key.— Proceeding, the juryman said that he had. had to stay away from business that morning in order to visit the I mortuary. He understood, when he went the previous day, that Dr. Aughton was in the hospital, and that he had given orders that the nurse must keep the key in ' her possession. When he went that morning he asked , for an explanation, and the doctor told him that they had heard in a vague way that somebody had been ask- ing for the key, but that there was some doubt. He ' told the doctor that he went in the usual way, and applied to the servant to open the door of the mortuary. The girl told him that she had been there seven years. and that she had always been trusted with the key to let the jurymen see the body whenever they came but he was distinctly told yesterday that he could not see ; the body. He then left the hospital, and told them he would report the matter to Mr. Brighouse.—The Coroner said the juryman had taken a proper course. He was sorry Mr. Abbott had been so inconvenienced. —Mr. Abbott: A patient was waiting on the steps with the key this morning.—The Coroner: Von have already done some good. Jurymen ought to have every assist- ance, and I will see into it.—. Sergeant Laing said the I matron of the hospital was away on holidays.—The , Coroner : Well, you will inquire into the matter and report to me.—Sergeant Laing : Yes, sir.

div.head: LETCHWORTH.
div.p: LETCHWORTH.
A Visit to the First Garden City.

[By CHAS. E. PARKER]. I have just returned from a visit to Letchworth and before the colours fade and the memories blur, let me set in order some of the impressions. We came away with a feeling that we have scarcely been in the same eountry which produces a sombre town like Warrington, even after it has been somewhat brightened by the workers and well-wishers of the Beautiful Warrington Society. Britishers do not value as they ought bright colours. We take life very seriously, ourselves, our homes, our work, our thoughts, our religion, even our pleasures are all dressed in sombre hues, and our spirits take their hues from their surroundings. Our laughter is forced, our gaiety has no spontaniety, we have lost the art of being merry, there is too little colour in our lives and in their surroundings, too little of that light that makes the mists of the firmament an ever changing panorama of brightness and glory. A good deal has been done at the first Garden City to bring colour and brightness back to one spot in England. I lost myself at times and thought I was again in California. The roofs are all covered with red tiles, the upper stories frequently covered with white pebble dash, the woodwork in many cases painted a bright colour, mostly green; there is an endless variety in detail of construction; every building has its own beauty, a beauty that is true because of its utility, and everything conforms to the general idea. Fortunately most of the estate is well wooded, and many of the houses have a background of lofty elms, in which the estate abounds. To unaccustomed English eyes the colouring may appear too vivid, the redness of the tiles and bricks too pronounced. If this be so, time, weather, lichen, and moss, will soon tone it down and give to all a mellowed richness. I spent the night at Letchworth, and was awakened early by the strokes of the hammer, and the pleasant ring of the trowel. Indeed I did not get away from these sounds all the time of my visit, they were build- ing everywhere. I visited many of the houses, saw the comfottable mansion that was to be the home of Sir John Gorst, and the humble cottage which was to bathe castle of some humble artizan.

The operations of the Garden City Tenants Limited was of special interest. Haying known the chairman, Henry Vivian for many years, I have watched with increasing interest the work of this practical idealist. While many have been talking, he has been working. Amongst the many interests of the recent General Election nothing gave me greater pleasure than to note the appreciation with which the workingmen of Warrington listened to the closely reasoned addresses of Mr. Vivian on the Fiscal Question from the worker's standpoint. It is pleasing to note that the duties and honours pertaining to the representation of Birkenhead in Parliament has not lessened the zeal of Henry Vivian in industrial co-onerative effort. He has found in the Garden City a favourable sphere for continuing, and it is hopea repeating, the success which his Tenants Association has achieved at Ealing. The Garden City Tenants Limited have already erected over one hundred work- men's cottages, besides building as contractors for private owners, several houses in the estate. The cottages of the Tenants Limited are grouped together ,in lots of about twenty. The one I visited enclosed 'on three sides a common green, the fourth side being formed.by the hedge and road. Each cottage lias its own garden both back and front, these covering‘ with the house about half an acre, and all face to the common green. There is a pleasing variety in the style of the cottages, this applies to the interior as well as the exterior. Most have bath with hot and cold water laid on. The houses so far are let as soon las finished, and with the additional works being established in the " City " there appears ample room I for continued development. Guardian " writes as follows :—" The news of Mr. James Charles's death comes as a blow to all lovers of good painting and sincerity in art. His training in Paris under Bouguereau was not a sound preparation for either quality, but Mr. Charles never allowed any influence long to interfere with his first-hand vision of things and his c!ear insight into the range of his own talent. His cottage interiors and rustic scenes have a fresh lyrical quality that is rare indeed in our time, and lie arrived at his effects by a direct and charming use of his m aterial. Save Mr. IPTaggart and Mr. H. Cameron, I cannot think of any contemporary who could communicate so convincingly the honest reality and fragrance os childhood. He was a regular contributor to the New English Art Club, to whose exhibitions his pictures were always notable additions. .0n the crowded walls of the Academy they seemed to lose much of their racy vigour and charming colour. Last year he paid a visit to Italy, and in his last- exhibited works he bad painted Italy with an absence of prepossession that one would have thought impossible to a man of our time. He was born at Warrington in 1851. Fame, in the popular sense, never came to him, but his reputation is well established in the good opinion of his brother artists, which is the opirtion that lives." Mr. Charles leavds a widow and family.
- ----- The usual votes of thanks concluded the meeting.

div.head: TAXATION OF LAND VALUES. _ Addresees by Mr. W. R. Lester and Others.
div.p: TAXATION OF LAND VALUES. _ Addresees by Mr. W. R. Lester and Others.

A meeting to consider " social questions and their solutions "was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- street, on Thursday evening. Mr. W H. Sherburn pre- sided over a small attendance and was supported by Mr. W. R. Lester, M.A., Mr. Skirrow,Bradford, Mr. Mc Hugh Birkenhead, and Mr. Ockel. Mr. LEsTER, in the course of a well-reasoned address said he did not intend to harrow their feelings .by a detailed description of some of the social conditions of the present day. All the evils which did exist were, he contended, at the bottom the outcome of the land question, and therefore if a remedy was to be found the land question must be tackled first, and the way to deal with it was by taxing the land values. In every society there were two kinds of values which grew— land and labour. Land formed a natural source of revenue instead of, as at present, the product of labour being taxed To-day we taxed labour and the product of labour, because we had failed at the outset to tap the natural source of revenue. In a word we taxed the man who by his indus- try found employment for other men, whilst the mere rent collector who did nothing was not touched. Was it to be wondered under such conditions—when enter- prise was encouraged by being fined by taxation—that .there was unemployment? (Applause). The landowner was encouraged to speculate in land, and hold it until the requirements of labour increased its value, for the increased value to be extracted from labour, Let the land be taxed according to its value, and the owner would be forced to put it into use with the result that there would be competi- tion to let land and rents would go down. To show how the withholding of land from the market produced unemployment, Mr. Lester instanced a coal mine with which he was connected. It was desired. he said, to double the output of the mine by sinkiag, a new shaft. Had this been done 200 more men would have been employed. So exhorhitant however, were the demands of the landlord in respect to royalties that as a business speculation the proposed extension would not have paid. It therefore had to be dropped with the result that at the mine they were employing 200 men less than would have been the case had the land- lord been induced by means of a tax to put his land in the market. He also submitted that the solution of the housing problem was embodied in the solution of the land problem. In New Zealand the imposition of a land tax resulted in a surprising boom in the building trade. The two things which caused unemployment and which were at the root of our social evils were the withholding of land from labour and the taxing of the product of labour. Let thee process be reversed and we would quickly reach a state which some called the milleniutn. (Applause). Mr. McHuott also delivered an address on the same subject. There was, he said, no relationship of which they could think which was more fundamental than that which obtained between man and land, and man could only exist as he had access to the source which was provided by his Maker for all his wants. The power which the landlord exercised over land was with- out limit and his ownership of the land, in effect involved the ownership of men. Every human being born into the world had an equal right to live and that. right involved an equal right to everthing which society required—land. Land without man had no value and therefore formed a natural source of taxation to the extent of the value which resulted from the existence of society. The revenue to be derived from the taxation of land, despite what was said to the contrasy, was sufficient, and even more than sufficient for all the pur- poses for which it was required. Mr.McHugh proceeded to details to illustrate this. Land in London he ex- plained had been sold for over £2OO a square -aard and in Liverpool for over £3O. Therefore:a° thought it was not unreasonable to place the average value of land in the towns and cities of 20s. per square yard. A tax of one per cent, on this would realize £190,000,000. per annum. With an equal tax on the 52,000,009 acres of agricultural land. valued of £1 an acres, brought the revenue to over £200.000,000 which he thought was more than sufficient. To adopt sncha tax would not be to impose an injustice on the landlords but would simply prevent the. present injustice which was done to the community at large. (Applause). In answer to a question Mr. Mc HUGH said it would be impossible for landlords to get the amount of the tax out of the tenant by means of an increased rent because of the competition which there would be to let the land.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Education I Committee was held at the Town Hall on Monday even- ing, under the presidency of Alderman Bennett. There were also present: —Aldermen Tinnion,and J.Evans,Coun- cillors Burton, Ellison, Dr. Joseph, Ball, Sankey, Lord, Pemberton, Wright, Evans and Maginn, the Revs. Neville Wilson and James Davies, Messrs. R. T. Fair- Clough, A. J. Jolley, C. S. Burgess, E. Plinston, J. Upson, G. Walker, T. S. Steel, J. Moore Murray I (director of education) and J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer).
THE RELATIVE COST OF ELENIENTARY AND
HIGHER EDUCATION. A DISCUSSION ABOUT PIANOS.

At a meeting of the Finance Committee authority was given for the allocation of the general payments for administration between the higher and elementary I education accounts in the proportion of one-sixth for the former and five-sixths for the latter. Permission was given for the use, after school hours, of the schools required by the Beautiful Warrington Society for an exhibition of plants and flowers grown by scholars, no charge being made upon the managers in respect of any cleaning, &c., necessary in consegnence thereof. The following scale of charges for the use of pianos supplied by the Committee to the various schools was adopted, viz, 6d. per occasion for each piano used for concerts Ste. ; and ss. per occasion for each piano used for dances. On the recommendation of the managers of the Ladies' School of Industry, it was resolved that Mrs. Margaret Dutton be appointed school keeper of the Ladies' School of Industry, at a salary at the rate of 5152 per annum ; her engagement to commence on a date to be hereafter fixed and to be determinable by one week's notice given either by or to the Committee. In moving the aloption of the minutes, Mr. JOLLEY said the first resolution was purely a book-keeping direction as to the method in which sundry administra- tive charges should be apportioned. The committee chose that particular proportion because it represented the relative expenditure on other matters under those two heads. In round figures, elementary education cost five times as much as the higher education of the town, so that it seemed a reasonable basis on which to charge the small general items. With regard to the use of the schools by the Beautiful Warrington Society, the committee were desirous to help forward the movement of which this was one of the develop- ments. Ile was sure he was only voicing the sentiments of his colleagues in wishing the Society every success. Alluding to the scale of charges fixed for the use of pianos, Mr. Jolley said a number of schools already bad pianos of their own. The scale did not relate to them, but only to the instruments supplied by the local authority. Councillor SANKEY seconded.

The Rev. JAMES liA.viEs maintained that in the case of a school wherea piano had already been supplied by the managers, when it was worn out, chiefly by the use of the day school, and replaced by the Education Com- mittee, the free use of the new instrument should be granted for parochial purposes. The CHAIRMAN: lam sure the Committee will con- sider that. Are you going to move an amendment? The Rey. JAMES DAVIES : Not if the resolution is understood in the sense I have indicated. Mr. JOLLEY : It cannot be understood in that sense. The Rev. JAMES DAVIES: Then I move that the resolution be not approved. Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH seconded. If a school bad its own piano he did not see why the Sunday school should be charged for the use of a new one when the I old instrument had been worn out by the day scholars. Mr. JOLLEY said that if the amendment were carried it would not make any difference to the result. The local authority could not break the law. If they pro- vided a piano for elementary school purposes they were I only discharging their duty. But they were not dis- charging their duty if they allowed it to be used for parochial or denominational purposes without charge. II The CHAIRMAN thought it would be as well for Mr. Davies to withdraw the amendment if Mr. Jolley thought it would be inoperative. The Rev. J. DAVIES : There is a fundamental principle involved, and I cannot see my way to with- draw it. On a vote being taken, the amendment was lost. The CHAIRMAN expressed his pleasure at the com- mittee's decision to allow the Beautiful Warrington Society to use the schools. It showed how heartily the committee were seconding the efforts that were being made to encourage in the minds of the children the love of plants and flowers. He was sure that at the show which would take place on Saturday they would have a pleasing object lesson of what had been done in that direction under difficult conditions. The Rev. JAMES Dkvles thought that those who carried on Sunday schools and other parochisl agencies were doing equally as much good as the Beautiful Warrington Society. If the schools ceuld be allowed free to that society, he did not see why the pianos could not be used free for parochial purposes under the conditions he had named. (Laughter.)
The minutes were approved. - THE SECONDARY SCHOOL STAFF. "TOO MANY CHANGES."

At a meeting of the School Management Committee the comments of the Managers of the Warrington Parochial school upon the report recently received from H.M. Inspector were received and noted. A report from the Board ot Education upon the St. George's (Infants') Council school was submitted, and, upon the recommen- dation of the Managers of the school, it was resolved, that Standard I. be continued in this school during the present educational school year. The Rev. Neville Wilson and the Director of Educa- tion were appointed to represent the Committee upon the Council of the Society for University Extension in Liverpool and District for the session 1906-7. It was resolved that the salary of Miss Beatrice M. Watkins. assistant Cookery Mistress, be increased from £9O to £95 per annum as from the 24th August, 1906. The Director was requested to prepare and submit for the consideration of the Committee a draft scale of salaries for the cookery teachers. A circular letter from the Board of Education,, in reference to the centres for the holding of the prelim- inary examination for the school teachers' certificate and the certificate examinaticn, was submitted, and the director was requested to communicate with the neighbouring local education authorities on the matter. It was resolved that the resignation of Miss Margaret B. Morton, L.L.A., assistant mistress at the Secondary school and Technical Institute, be accepted, her engage- ment to terminate from the 31st August, 1906. The 'action of the director in issuing advertisements inviting applications for the vacant post was approved, and it wars resolved,that Mr. Councillor Lord,Mr. John Upson,' the Rev. Neville Wilson. and the chairman of the com- mittee (the Rev. Canon Stevenson) be appointed a sub- committee to consider the applications received. A report by the head master of the Secondary school unon the work of the free students during the year 1905-6 was submitted, but consideration thereof was deferred for further information. It was noted that the Board of Education had acceded to the committee's application for the loan of some of the National Competition Works of 1906, and that the same would be lent to the committee from the 28th September to the 2nd October. The Rev. NEVILLE WnsoN moved the adoption of the minutes. With regard to the reports on the War- rington Parochial and St. George's schools,the managers had undertaken to give them their best attention and any causes of complaint would, as far as possible, be immediately remedied. Alluding to the increase of salary to Miss Watkins, Father Wilson said that at present there was no scale of salaries for cookery teachers and the committee had undertaken to consider the question of introducing one. Tbe present increase did not raise the teacher's salary beyond what WrtS about the average sum paid en teachers of that class and of that amount of experience. Councillor Dr. JOSEPH seconded. Mr. PLINs•roN said be would like to know whether it was the intention of the committee when vacancies occurred to take into consideration the appointment of some of the ex-pupil-teachers who vt erent present out of employment in the borough. Unfortunately there were a number of them in that position and he believed theyfelt rather sore about it. With regard to the resignation of Miss Morton, he had beard a great deal said in days gone by both in committee and outside as to the Secondary school not being as useful and doing as good a .Avork as it ought to do. He maintained that that was largely due to the fact that they had had changes at the school which ought not to have taken place. They heard sometimethat the salaries of the teachers were rather too high, but it seemed a strange thing that teachers who were working in the Secondary school should be worth so much more money to smaller authorities than they were to Warrington. He thought that if the Com- mittee endeavoured by some means to retain the present staff they would raise the calibre of the school and obtain far greater results than if they were contin- ually losing teachers who had done excellent work. He felt sorry that these vacancies occurred. The present one was the third or fourth within a few months, and he believed the changes were owing to the fact that other authorities, many of them smaller than Warrington, were paying better salaries. He did not believe in the policy of endeavouring to get good work out of people and paying very little for it. They were told sometimes that they were spending the rate- payers' money very freely and "efficiency with economy' was continually preached. Let them endeavour to get good work, retain the staff they had, and Day them proper wages for their duties. Tho Rev. NEviwt WILSON said that ex-pupil teacher's would be employed when vacancies which they could

GOD'S LITTLE LIGHTS.

A little child lay in its crib and sobbed tte- cause it was afraid of the dark. And its father, in the room below, heard the sobs, and came up and said, "What ails you my dearie, and why do you cry?" And the child said, "Oh, father, I am afraid of the dark. Nurse says lam too big to have a taper; but all the corners are full of dreadful blackness, and I think there are things in them with eyes that would look at me if I looked at them; and if they looked at me,l should die. Oh, father, why is it dark? Why is there such a terrible thing as darkness? Why cannot it be always day?" The father took the child in his arms and carried it downstairs and out into the summer night. "Look up, dearie," he said, in his strong, kind voice. "Look up, and see God's little lights!" The little one looked up, and saw the stars spangling the blue veil of the sky; bright as candles they burned, and yellow as gold. "Oh, father!" cried the child, "what are those lovely things?" "Those are stars," said the father. are God's little lights." "But why have I never seen them before?" "Because you are a very little child, and have never been out in the night before." " Can I see the stars only at night, father?" "Only at night, my child." "Do they only come then, father?" "No; they are always there, but we cannot gee them when the sun is shining." "But, father, the darkness is not terrible here : it is beautiful."
"Those
"Yes, dearie, the darkness is always beauti- ful, if we will only look up at the stars, in- stead of into the corners."
"PRIDE GOES BEFORE A FALL." Adolphus Stuart Fitz-James Was haughty beyond any saying, And he laughed to scorn all the games His comrades delighted in playing. He'd walk with his nose in the air,

And, if ever a school-fellow meeting, A cool supercilious stare Was all he vouchsafed as greeting. Mut one day, with his nose quite beyond Its usual high standard of being, He walked right into a pond, Tat of course he had no chance of seeing, And when he at length crawled out, He was quite an elegant figure; For in truth he was just about As black as the blackest old nigger. From that day to this, so one states, Adolphus's pride has krov,-11 mellow, And he plays every game with his mates, And is voted a very good fellow!

div.head: INDIA'S SACRED CATTLE.
div.p: INDIA'S SACRED CATTLE.

Hindoos regard the zebu, an ox with a fatty hump on its back, above the shoulders, as a sacred animal, and the creature is allowed to do pretty much as it pleases. Should it meet a native cart or carriacre in a narrow street, the vehicle must be dra,n to one side in order that the bull may no be disturbed. Happy will the driver be should the animal thrust its head into the carriage window. This is a piece of good fortune in his opinion, no matter what the English " fare " inside may think. As the zebu goes along it often helps itself to eatables exposed for sale on stalls and bar- rows, and the poor owner dare not interfere with it even if he would. Sometimes an ox will lie dowu before a house door, and until it moves of its own accord, no one may pass in or out, because it would be a high misdemeanour to step over the body of the lazy but sacred crea- ture.

Funeral of the Late Mr. John Taylor. In the presence of many relatives and friends the funeral took place at the Cemetery on Sunday of the late Mr. John Taylor, grocer and provision dealer, of 19,Allen-street.- Representatives of the Forster-street Gospel Hall, in the work connected with which he as greatly interested, were present. The last rites were performed by Mr. Joseph Whitehouse, assisted by Messrs. Harry Goldsmith and F. Broadhurst, of Waterloo. The chief mourners were : —Mrs. Taylor (widow), Messrs. John W. Taylor and Fred Taylor (sons), Mrs. Winstanley, Mrs. Broadhurst and Miss Elizabeth Taylor (daughters), Messrs. J. Broadhurst and Winstanley (sons-in-law), Mrs. J. W. Taylor and Mrs. F. Taylor (daughters-in-law), and Mr. Peter Taylor (brother), and Mr. Joseph Sudfow (nephew). Other mourners included Mr. J. Skelland, Mr. Newman and Mr. J. McNab, of Liverpool. The bearers were Messrs. Wooldridge, Green, Roden, Rudge Nichol and Reynolds. A large number of floral tributes were sent.

Junior Conservative Drive.

The third and last drive a the season promoted by the Junior Conservative Association took place on Tuesday evening to Arley Park, and was a great success. About fifty vehicles were requisitioned to convey the 1,500 or more members and friends who *veiled themselves of the opportunity of visiting this charming Cheshire resort. Among those who accom- panied the party were Mr. E. Draper (chairman of the club), Alderman Smethurst, Mr. Segar Owen, Mr. W. L. Williams (chairman of the association), Mr. W. Rogers, Mr. William Holbrook (registration agent, and Mr. Herbert Hayes (manager of the club). The weather was ideal and the outing was thoroughly enjoyed. The outward journey was made via.,Latch- ford, Grappenhall, and Appleton Thorn, and after crossing the beautiful Arley Park, the party returned by 13udworth and Stretton. When a short distance from the last named place a halt was made to enable the marshals and others to light the Chinese and Japanese lanterns which were attached to the vehicles, and the effect produced was exceedingly striking. Warrington was safely reached a few minutes after eleven o'clock,

I shall have a very hard task to decide which are the prettiest, as they are all so very nice. I am very pleased to welcome Elsie Timmins and. HOW I SPENT MY BANK-HOLIDAY.
I awoke early on Monday morning, and anxiously looked at the weather, for we had arranged to have a picnic at South_ Haven, near Studland. _ _
The sky was rather cloudy, but it. was a sign for a hot day. We had breakfast early, and then got ready our lunch and tea to take with us.

Our party of eleven arrived at the Quay at 11 o'clock. We had hired the ferry-boat, so that we had plenty of room to mova about, and not get cramped. A gentleman and my father rowed us, and a sailing-boat towed us some little distance. We arrived at South Haven about 12 a'clock, and as we all felt hungry, we had lunch at once. After lunch we paddled and cackled; the cockles were in the sand and were very large, they are not like the mud ones. Then some of us had a swim. When we grew tired of the water, some went for a long walk. While we were gone the tide went out Quickly and left the boat on the sand, and we had to push and pull to get it off, for it is a very heavy boat. Then we all sat down till 5.30, and read books and ate chocolates. We got in the boat again, and rawed over to Sand- banks to have tea.

After tea we sat on the Hills; we had a lovely view from them. It was 7.30 when we reached the boat to start for home; the sun was just sinking, and the water was lovely. We all in turn rowed the boat home.. Reached the Quay about 8.30 o'clock. Every one enjoyed Bank-holiday very much.
From AM,IE KEIVDILL.L

A YOUNG FOLK'S ALPHABET. A was for Alice, the belle of the ball, B was the Banquet, laid out in the hall. C was the Captain who sought for her hand, D were the Dances he hoped to demand. E was young Edward, who loved her in vain, F her Flirtations, which caused him much

Q were the Questions which joined them for. life, R was the Ring which made Alice his wife. 6 were the Speeches made through the day, t were the Tears Alice shed by the way. , Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sending you a piece of poetry, which is called—

MABEL'S SIXPENCE. Oh! Dolly, Dolly, can it be true, That I have a sixpence to spend on you? Yes, Dolly, dear, when I go to town, buy you a lovely blue gown; And a broad red sash and a pair of shoes, The very prettiest I shall choose. A velvet hat with long, white feathers, A pr-a-sol for sunny weather. Oh, Dolly, how gay you'll be! And Mabel danced about with glee. The very next day, Mabel went to town To buy the stuff for Dolly's gown. But alas! alas! for the broad red sash, rhe bright blue dress took all the cash. No money was left for hat and feather, Shoes, or sunshade, for summer weather. DORM THACKER. Aged 8 years'.
-4- THE KETTLE AND THE CLOCK.

In a kitchen over a fire stood. a. kettle. It ,hought itself nice ttncl new, as it was kept very shiny, but really it was very old. Just above it on a shelf was a clock. This doe had done its work in that house for year an.d still it kept on "tick, tick." It was oh. too. "Bother that clock," said the kettle. out night, to the poker; "it worries me out :15; my life, with its 'tick, tick,' all the time.' only do my duty," answemd the poor clock. A few minutes passed, and then the poker broke the silence by saying, "Why, the clock has stopped." "I am so glad," said the kettle gladly; "I expect it is broken, so then to-morrow it will be thrown .away." But the kettle was wrong, for the next day the master of ill/house wound the clock up, and it went on again. That same night the servant dis- covered the kettle ran. It was therefore thrown away.. When it lay in the dust-heap, Lt •began to feel lonely, and thought, "It ..3erves me right, for wishing the clock to be put here." From,. LTJCY PETERS.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sanding you a piece of poetry, which I made. r,p myself. It called:
IT MATTERS, MUCH.

It matters little where I was 'born, If my parents were rich or poor, Whether they shrank at the cold world's scorn, Or walked in the path of wealth secure. But whether I live an honest girl, And hold my integrity firm in my clutch, I tell you, my brother, as plain as I can, It matters much.

It matters little how long I stay In this world of snriow and care, Whether to-morrow I'm called away, , Or I live t,lll my bones and pate are bare,. But whether I do the best I can, To soften the weight of adversity's touch, On the faded check uf my fellow man— ' • It matters much.

It matters little where is my grave, On land or on the sea, By flurling brook, or 'neath stormy wave, It really is naught to me; . But whether the Angel of God comes down, And marks my brow with his loving touch, As one that shall wear the 'Victor's Crown, It matters much. JANIE PASSMORF..

div.head: Price of Soap —Surprise for: Retailers.
div.p: Price of Soap —Surprise for: Retailers.

- • The price of soap is likely to be raised shortly This month three of the largest arms of soap-boners in the country —Messrs. Lever Brothers, Messrs. Jos. Crosfield and Sons, and Nfessra. Watson and Sons have sent round a circular notifying their customers that owing to the advance in thet cost of raw materials the price of soap must be raised in a corresponding degree. The present advance will affect only the retail salesmen, but it is announced that, unless the cost of raw mqterial drops to its former level, the retail prices of soap must be raised. Messrs. Lever Brothers' circular thus explains the situation : "During this year a gradual rise has taken place in the price of raw materials, which is now Neal to a rise of £3 per ton on the above soaps, and as this advance in raw materials appears to be of a more settled character than such rises usually have been, it. is too serious to be ignored. It is, of course, quite i impossible for us to make a corresponding rise n the price of soap. Therefore, we have made our rise only is. to Is. 3d. per gross or per cwt., and are hopeful that with this rise we may be able to grapple with the situation. Should, however, the rise in raw materials 'continue to be still further accentuated, the situation could then only be met by a permanent rise in the retail price of soap." Druids' Lodge Meeting. - - • -

The monthly meeting of the " Druids Camp" lodge was held at the Higher Angel Hotel, Butter- market-street, on Saturday night, under the chairman- ship of Bro. Samuel Hankey. The Lodge was honoured with a visit by the District Officers, includ- ing the Grand Master Bro. John Woods, the District Treasurer, Bro. Robert Perdue, and Bro. Samuel Dunbobin, P.D.G.M. After several new members had been initiated, the Chairman called on the Grand Master to present Bro. Thomas Darbyshire with an illuminated certificate of merit for his services. The Grand Master said it gave him great pleasure to do so, , as Bro. Darbyshire, although only a young member, had shown his great ability in looking after the interest of the Lodge. (Applause.) Bro Darbyshire said he was gratified to End that his efforts to do his duty to his neighbours were appreciated, and the pre- sentation would serve as an incentive to him to do his best'in the future. There was a duty that every man owed to himself and those depending on him, and that was to make some provision for the day of sickness, and lie would add that they owed a duty to one another. (Applause). Bro. Samuel Dunbobin then presented Bro. Thomas Jones with an illuminated certificate of merit, and expressed the pleasure it had given him to be present that evening at the interest- ing ceremony, and to see so large a gathering of young members taking an interest in the Lodge. Bro. Jones returned thanks. A vote of thanks having been I accorded to the District Officers, the rest of the even- ing was 'spent in listening to a musical pragramme.
LAWN TENNIS, CROQCTET, and other outdoor sports.—J. S. GARLAND, 51,Bridge-st.—Advt.
Appleton !Me Club.

'The third monthly competition of the present season/was held at the range last Saturday. There was a good attendance, the majortty of those present entering for the various competitions. The medal competition, which is fired with the service rifle, con- sists of 10 shots at a stationery target, 3M. bull, and 10 shots'at a disappearing figure target ; the distance being 100 yards, and the possible score 100 points. At all competitions except the forthcoming one on the 22nd of September, money prizes are awarded; the first prize on the latter date being the bronze medal, which is supplied annually by the National Rile Association. , The winner of the first prize last Satur- day was Mr. T. Wilcox, with a score of 84 ; Mr. B. Fairclough taking the second; with a score of 79 points. The Open Sweep-stakes .consists of five shots with any rifle, at 100 yards, 3m. bell ; the highest possible score being 20 points. The results were : Ist prize, Mr. B. Fairclough, who made 16; 2nd prize, Mr. J. Wilcox, with a score of 15 points. In the Members'. Stakes, which is shot with any rifle at a distance of 100 yards, with a 6in, bull, and comprises seven shots in addition to a sighting shot, the highest possible score being 28, the results were :—Mr. B. Fairolough, Ist prize with 27 points, and Mr. A. Warburton 2nd, with 25 points.— On Saturday, the 18th of August, two members of the club were successful in qualifying for the " Rifleman's Miniature Certificate," which is issued by the secretaries of rifle clubs under the authority of the National Rifle Association. Competitions fired with miniature rifles, at various distances from 20 up to 100 yards. The distance adopted by the Appleton Club, are 25 yards with 7-Sin, bull, 50 yards with a lin. bull, and 100 yards with a nin. bull. Ten shots are fired at each distances, or 20 at one distance, and 10 at another, or the whole may be fired at one distance. The highest possible score is 150 points, but it is necessary to make 114 to gain the certificates. The winners were Mr. A. Down, with a score of 123, and Mr. W. Stewart with 121 points. Several other members came within a narrow margin of the necessary score.

The remedy here is obvious, viz., to make it obligatory on owners of coalfields to develop them or allow others to do so, and a sound tax on the value of the fields would accomplish this, with the result that unemployed miners then finding employment would buy clothes, f )od and furniture, thus in their turn, giving employment in other trades. The previously unemployed workers in these other trades would complete the circle of exchange by buying the extra coal produced by the miners. And to leave the particular for the general, it is clear that this stimulus has only to opergite\ all round and the demand for labour would infinitely• grow over the whole field of industry, sr removing the primary cause of unemployment, over-crowding and sweated labour. This being accomplished it would surely then be time enough to see whether any call remained for the hundred and one secondary reforms so many now demand. A fundamental wrong involves other wrongs. If we may venture an appeal to progressives of all shades it would be —Concentrate on the reform which goes to the root. Overthrow land -monopoly through taxation. When monopoly is gone we shall at last have established a sound foundation on which society may build to heights now undreamed of.
WELL-MERITED SENTENcE.

At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, before Dr. Fox and Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, Dominick O'Connor,who stated that he was employed at the docks in Liverpool, pleaded not guilty to a charge of insult- ing females in Winwick-road. The Chief Constable said it was a most painful case. The prisoner deliber- ately and repeatedly insulted several women and also behaved in a disgraceful manner in the presence of children.—Evidence was given by Mrs. Griffiths and her daughter and Mrs. Clay, 166, inwick-road.—Prisoner said he had had too much drink Pnd it affected him. He asked the Bench to be lenient with him as his wife was in Winwick Asylum—he was going to see her at the time—and he had three children.—The Bench committed prisoner to gaol for three months' hard labour—the highest sentence they could impose, and thanked Mrs. Clay and Mrs.Griffiths for the action they had taken in the matter. s

div.head: Funeral of Adjutant Cooper.
div.p: Funeral of Adjutant Cooper.

The funeral at Warrington Cemetery on Saturday afternoon of Adjutant Cooper, of the Sanation Army, who died after a short illness in the fever hospital in Aitkin-street, was the occasion of a striking demon- stration of r6spect. In addition to the relatives, a large party of Salvationists joined in the funeral pro- cession to the Cemetery, and the Dead March in " Saul "was played very impressively by the band or the corps. A large number of people had assembled at the Cemetery, and at the graveside Colonel Wilson and Brigadier Mcllinnies delivered short addresses. Hymns were sung by Major and Mrs. Cloude. Many choice floral tributes were placed over the grave. -

div.head: LITTLE BOY BLUE.
div.p: LITTLE BOY BLUE.

The little toy dog is covered with dust, , But sturdy and staunch he stands; And the little toy soldier is red with rust, And his musket moulds ii. his hands. Time was when the little toy dog was new And the soldier wae passing fair, And that was the time when our little boy blue Kissed them and put them there.

" Now don't you go till I come," he said, "And don't you make any noise"; ;So toddling off to his trundle-bed, He dreamt of the pretty toys. And as he was dreaming, an angel song Awal:ened our little .boy blue— Oh, the years are many, the years are long, But, the littlettoy friends are *rue. Ay, faithful to little boy blue they stand, Eacla in the same old place; Awaiting the touch of a little hand, Thc iO of a little face. And th:v wonder, as waiting these long years through, In :Ile dust of that little 'chair, What has become of our little boy blue Since he kissed them and put them there. H. B.
