NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Anthors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith.

Right to Work Committee. Sir,—At a recent meeting of the Right to Work Committee, the following resolution was unanimously passed :—" That this Committee deplores the niggardly way in which the Government has met the claims of the Unemployed, in view of the inadequacy of the grant of £200,000 to meet the necessities of the case ; and further it protests against the refusal of the Govern- ment to amend the Unemployed Workmen's Act of last session in such a manner as to confer greater powers upon the local authorities, especially to provide work." —Yours etc., JAS. HAMPSON, Secretary. 55, Garibaldi-street-

div.head: " The Proposed Amalgamation of Labour."
div.p: " The Proposed Amalgamation of Labour."

Sir,—Seeing you have been good enough to give somewhat prominent ventilation to the above question, may I be allowed just a few words by way of comment? To begin with, I see it stated in your report that the Joint Trades and Labour Conference held on the 16th inst was an L.R.C. Conference, and that the conclusions arrived at, are referred to as L.R.C. demands. I need hardly say, sir, that this way of putting it is not pre- cisely correct,for the L.R.C. had no more to do with the Conference than the Right to Work Committee,and as a matter of fact neither of there committees had half as much to do with it as the Trades Council itself. Your report also goes on to say that the situation is serious, and that there is a likelihood of a split etc. Here again, your conclusions are not warranted, because the situation is a long way from being serious, neither is there the least sign or fear of a split. I am bound to admit, that with the help of a wee bit of sophistry an outsider might be led to believe that such is the case, but, disclaiming all egotism, I am glad to say there is sufficient commonsense among all sections of Labour, to prevent this important question being played into the hands of the enemy. With so much confusion in the minds of the voters, and over- lapping in the management of affairs, it is inevitable that if progress is to be made,these obstacles must be removed once for all. Calm and thoughtful discussion is necessary certainly, but there need be no disruption, for the simple reason that if the recom- mendations of the Conference are not accepted, existing arrangements need not be disturbed. Personally, I strongly contend that the only logical solution of a very illogical and complicated system of control and management, such as we now tacitly possess is the formation of a Labour Association, with a strong Council meeting monthly and an Executive meeting bi-weekly. Affiliated to the National Labour Party. this new body would be potentially powerful and useful in all matters relating to labour, whether political, industrial or social, national or local. I cannot for the life of me see what tangible or sensible objection can be taken to this suggestion, neither can I conceive anything being done by the Trades Council, Labour Representative Committee, or Right to work Committee, which could not he equally well done, and at considerable less waste of time and money by a Labour Association. As to the question of independence and status of membership, let them be thrashed out and voted upon, and if there is a sufficient majority to warrant the thing being carried out, let us proceed with it, if not, then I counsel further existence. Yours truly,
30th August, 1906.

div.head: DELEGATE.
div.p: DELEGATE.
The Condition of the Masses.

_ Sir,—The problem of how to raise the lower classes to a higher plane of thinking and living, has been occu- pying the attention of men and women for generations. Whether in the estimation of those who are struggling and striving after a better order of existence we are any nearer the millennium or not is a debatable question •, but I believe it is generally admitted by all thoughtful men and women, that the present generation is a great improvement upon its predecessor. Bat while this may be so, it is open to question whether our present method of regenerating mankind is the best which could be devised in the interest of humanity, of pro- gress and happiness. It is a query whether the present methods of piling upon humanity a burden of taxation whim seems to be growing upon what it feeds upon, and getting heavier and heavier year by year are wise methods. As an illustration of this we might point to Birmingham, which is considered to be the best governed City in the empire, and point to its debt of 15 millions, with its rateable value of three millions, where every child which is born into the city owes a debt of I ,E3O which it has done nothing to contract. From this it would appear that humanity at least in this England of ours will have an old man of the sea on its shoulders which it will find it no little difficulty to cast off. Municipal apathy is largely responsible for this condition of things, and until you can get your citizens to display a deeper interest in local matters, you will never get substantial and beneficial reforms introduced into your municipal life. It is only by in- dustrious canvassing that you can induce proportion to come and record their votes. You must first train your country men and women,lto take an intelligent interest in the affairs of their town and country before you can hope to bring about those real reforms, which should I make for the better education and comfort and leisure of your fellow men and women. We shall never bring about this most desirable condition of things unless we commence with the children at school. This matter of educating the rising generation in the responsibility. of Citizenship, should commence with the child at school. I Both schools and churches, should take upon themselves , the responsibility of teaching the sacredness of the franchise. I would make it obligatory upon every voter to exercise his power, and where that power is not used, he should have it withheld. A Curious condition of our municipal government to-day, is the haphazard way in which men are chosen to manage the affairs of our town and cities. The majority of men selected for this work are untrained, and make very amateur councillors, whose sole ambition is to gain some little local distinction, but who have never taken hold of the great motive, which should be the ever prompting incentive, viz., a service of sacrifice for the community. Sometimes men of this character are chosen, and are willing to make financial sacrifices in the interest of their town, which are reflected in the broader and better government of the town or city in which they are interested. It is very difficult to get into municipal life, men who could best administer the work, and who would be willing to retire from money making earlier in life— (which money is only left to demoralise their children)— and devote their experience and knowledge to the improvement of their native town ; our present methods of selecting men to fill our public offices are too narrow end not at all calculated to get the best brains and ci•-iracter to discharge public duties. My idea of gelocting men for our Town Council or Board of

Guardians, would be to hold a large public meeting where all shades of political and social life would be represented,and for names to be asked for,and submitted to take it out of the hands of either Tory, Liberal,Non- Trader or Independent Labour Party, to narrow down the selection to their own colour. This would broaden eut the selection and make for better municipal govern- ment. Instead of this a handful of Tories mske a I selection, a Committee of Liberals do the same, or a select few of the Non-Traders, or the Independent Labour Party take the same course, and the one so selected is run in the interest of the party who has made the selection. No party which organizes itself with the purpose of further class legislation, can be broad enough or charitable enough to represent the electors in this Country, or to do good Municipal work —Class legislation, whether it be in the interest of the very poor, the middle class, or the rich, is pernicious, and is not calculated to mske for the common good. You can have no abiding reform which sets class against class. Your public men should be chosen not because they are rich, or because they belong to the labouring classes, but because their chief qualifications are the deep and intense interest they take in humanity as a whole, and who can be trusted to do what is right and just in the common interest of all, and whose great ideal is to raise humanity to a higher plane of living and thinking.
I

There was a large attendance at a meeting held at Bridge Foot on Thursday evening under the auspices of the Tndependent Labour Party in support of " Votes for Women." Miss Christabel Pankhurst, L.L.B. and Miss Annie Kenney were announced as the principal speakers, but owing to her voice having given way, Miss Kenney was unable to be present. Councillor Stott presided over the proceedings which were followed with great interest. div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
[By " Ovalist.]
My football annual is nearly sold out, and I am gratified at the welcome it has received from the snorting public of Warrington.

To-morrow (Saturday) the football season opens, and most of the crack clubs in both codes will be hard at work in the struggle for points and glory. Perhaps I should have put the glory first, at the risk of sacri- ficing a certain amount of accuracy, but the fact remains that in these days of competition football the points are the primary, consideration.

It is by no means certain that Warrington will get any points as the result of the opening encounter. Leigh are again Warrington's first opponents, and as the match is at Leigh the odds must be considered on their side somewhat. Still it is worth 'recollecting that Warrington won at Leigh two years ago by 16 points to 2in the opening match, and last season triumphed at Warrington by 7 points to nil on the first Saturday in September. The omens are, then, pretty good for the opening day. Leigh men probably count upon the facts that they are the present League champions, and that they defeated Warrington twice later on in last season. Anyhow there should be a rare struggle at Mather-lane, and personally I think Warrington stand a very good chance of coming out on top.

The practice games have shown that most of the Warrington men are in capital trim, and are also adapting themselves smartly to the thirteen a side game and the new touch rule. Play is now so much faster and continuous that "bellows to mend " will soon be the complaint of the untrained player and he will be compelled to stand down in favour of a fitter competitor. There is not the same chance of hiding in the ruck and talAng a breather as heretofore, and the probability is that absolute necessity will do more towards bringing about real systematic training than all the stringent rules ever formed and broken. So far the practice games have pleased the great majority of spectators, who welcome the reduced number of scrummages and stoppages. But the changes cannot be voted a success straight away. They must bear the test of competition football before they are applauded to the skies.

Leigh will be practically at full strength for the encounter, but Dunbavin is an important absentee. The broken shin-bone he sustained last season has not got strong yet, and his place at half back will be taken by the ex-Warringtonian, Burgess. Leigh's selected thirteen areA as follows : Clarkson, full back; Sam Johnson, Tom Johnson, Bennett, Neville, three- quarters; Burgess, Whittaker, half backs; Berry, Blackburn, Lee, O'Neil, Webster,Winstanley,forwards.

The Warrington team have been chosen as follows; Berry, full back : Fish, Isherwood, Taylor, and Harris, threequarters ; Hockenhall and Lees, half backs ; Preston, Boardman, Thomas, Naylor, Heath, and Harmer, forwards. This is a strong side, and with anything like the old-time combination ought to give a satisfactory account of itself.

The " A "team will set the ball rolling at Wilders- pool against Widnes Rangers, and the following thirteen have been picked. to do duty : Knight, full back ; Jordan, Cartwright, Dickinson, and Landor, threequarters ; Davies and Brooks, half backs ; Jolley, Swift, Bradshaw, Barker, Forster, and Boardman, for- wards. The trial canter with the Widnes boys should produce a good margin of points. By the way, a trial is being given to three local lads in Landor, Barker, and Boardman, the latter being a younger brother of the county forward. Lambert, the promising junior half-back, is slightly injured, but will soon be fit again. The first combination match at home is not till the last Saturday in the month, when Broughton Rangers "A" are due at Wilderspool.

div.head: Association Football.
div.p: Association Football.

The fixtures for to-day in the Warrington and District League Competition for the Dodds Championship Shield are as follows : FIRST DIVISION. Latchford Christ Church v. Palatine, referee, J. Lloyd. Castner Kelner v. Orford Barracks. referee, F. Clegg. Rylands v. Golborne, referee, J. Mather. SECOND DIVISION.
Latchford Crescents v. Orford A.F.C., referee A. Owen.
Cricket.

Warrington I=l a narrow escape from defeat on Saturday, time alone preventing their Bolton visitors from recording a victory. The finish was an exciting one, such as the spectator delights in. Warrington had all been dismissed for 105, and the Bolton score was only one short of that total when the last over was bowled. To the joy of the Warringtonians E. A. Connor brought off a splendid catch from Callon's delivery to Nicholson, and the situation was just saved. For once the luck was with Warrington, who had indeed reason to congratulate themselves on averting disaster.

The feature of the Warrington innings was a fine dis- play by that promising young cricketer, W. Richardson. He was at the wicket for two hours and fifteen minutes and his batting exhibited the utmost patience and res- traint. The wicket was far from favourable to the bats- man, but he was content to a%Nait his opportunities and made the most of them. His 45 included two threes and nine twos. The other chief scorers were J. Callon (23) and J. Thompson (16).

On the Bolton side, A. Ward, the old Lancashire player, was in. grand form. He gave no chances and carried out his bat after compiling 60. He also did most effective work with the ball, capturing 4 wickets at the very low cost of 9 runs.
--- Ctesswell came oat with the best bowling analysis for Warrington, accounting for 3 wickets for 19 runs.

-- -- Warrington 2nd triumphed over Great Moor (Stock- pdtt), thanks mainly to the bowling of B. IV. Bennett and D. Plinston who crot the home side out for 42. Bennett had the splendid anilysis of seven wickets for 15 runs, whilst Plinston took three wickets at a cost. of a dozen runs.

Grappenhall 2nd gained a victory at the expense of Altrincharn Wesleyans 2nd. There was nothing very striking about the match—except the lowness of the scores—J. Mottrana (11 not out) having the best total.

Stretton and Appleton had no difficulty in disposing of Oughtrington Park 2nd. For the Winners J. Johnson gays a capital display making 51 in faultless style. The home team fared bkdly against the deliveries of J. Johnson and G. Hatton,the former taking three wickets for five runs, and the later six for eleven.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

To-day (Saturday) will witness the semi-final in con- nection with the Warrington Works Competition and an excellent afternoon's play is promised. The com- peting teams are L. & N.W. and Fletcher Russel, and P. &K. (No. 1) and Rylands (No. 1). In regard to one of the engagements it is generally expected that last year's champions, P. & K., will again qualify for the final. The other match contains a greater degree of uncertainty though the railway men should win. True their form so far has not been particularly brilliant hut there are rumours of changes in the team which will strengthen the weak spots and make the combination more uniform. Fletcher Russel however mean to make their presence felt and with every hope of victory they will give the ex-champions a good game and the match will not be decided without a good struggle.

On Saturday P. and K. triumphed over Crosneld's though the losers put up an exceedingly good fight. P. and K. at the outset carried all before them and after four games led 60-31. On the next two games Crosfields claimed one point so that the position prac- tically remained unchanged, and then the champions again forged ahead and carried the score to 102-69. it was at this stage that Crosfield's caused not a little uneasiness to the leaders by running away and drawing within seven points of the leaders score. The effort was, however, too great to be maintained and P. and K. qualified for the final by ten chalks.

The competition for the consolation prizes continues to produce exciting finishes and on Saturday three games were decided. In one of these, C.LC., playing against Whitecross, had particularly hard lines. They opened badly but a smart recovery sent them to the front and with five men off the green they led by five points. The sixth game was never decided as Sunder- land failed to put in an appearance so that, though beaten on the games decided,Whitecross claimed a walk over, and consequently, als) the match.

Hutchings Tannery, in their match with Fletcher Russell (No. 2), opened, metaphorically speaking with a flourish of trumpets, and rapidly acquired a lead of eleven points. Judge their dismay when they were badly let down by Robinson and the totals were made equal. Robinson's defeat was only the forerunner of

div.head: what was still worse as the tanners appeared to lose all heart, and though they made a final effort, they were beaten,
div.p: what was still worse as the tanners appeared to lose all heart, and though they made a final effort, they were beaten,

Rylands (No. 4) did not win without a struggle. The first game went in their honour, but their lead was immediately almost 'reduced to vanishing point, in fact a little later the position of the teams was reversed and P. and K. (No. 3) went to the front by two points This position was maintained until the end, when Whittaker ran away from Holbrook, and gave the gas stove men the victory.
Two teams, Castle Rubber and Monks Hall (No. 2) were awarded byes, as the teams against which they were drawn to play did not put in an appearance.

The first annual main open to Oddfellows of the War- rington District was decided on Saturday. The number of entries, though large, was not so great es was expected but nevertheless the proceedings can be regarded as highly successfol. For one thing there was a pleasant combination of driving and bowling, waggon- ettes and similar vehicles being chartered to convey the competitors to the Rope and Anchor Inn,Woolston, over the green attached to which the the main was decided. There was an excellent display of trundling talent and some excellent work was seen. The first prize went to T. Bolton, a prominent member of the Cemetery Hotel Club and who as a rule plays a con- sistently good game and one which is above the average. On Saturday he was in his best form though in the final J. Brooks ran him close and was only defeated by the odd point.

As was expected the Senior Conservatives of Warring- ton revenged themselves upon the Altrincham Club for defeat which they sustained on the Altrincham green. The return 'match was decided at Warrington on Satur- day and the home team carrying all before them won by 159 points, claiming on the two matches a balance of Si points.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

The season is rapidly drawing to a close and wheelers are making the most of their opportunities of visiting their favourite haunts. On Saturday the members of the Warrington Cycling Club held their annual fishing match at Acton Bridge and twenty-three enthusiasts put in an appearance fully armed for the fray. The War- rington Anglers' Association kindly allowed the club to fish in their waters and about two hours good sport was enjoyed. The first prize was won by W. Brown (weight about llh.), the second by A. G. Robertson and the third by J. E. Bertles. Tea was served at the Leigh Arms and afterwards a smoking concert was held.

-- The final Tuesday night run was held on Tuesday evening and closed with a "smoker." at the Sankey Chapel House. The event was a great success, forty or fifty being present when Mr. F. Fieldhouse took the chair. There was a grand array of talent and their services were greatly, appreciated. Mesqrs. J. L. Davenport, W. A. Clay, J. Emson, J. B. Poole, H. M. Ashton, G. H. Smith. and F. Fieldhouse all contributed to an excellent programme, the accompaniments being 'played by Mr. A. Warburton. A most enjoyable even- ing was spent and the closing night run of 1901 must be classed as one of the best held for some years.
To-day (Saturday) is President's and Ladies' Day and the club will visit Chester and Ecoleston Ferry.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: TOWN COUNCIL.
Business of the Next Meeting,

The monthly meeting of the Town Council will be held on Tuesday when the following,among other busi- ness, will be dealt with. Arsorrous' REPORTS. The reports of the Mayor's Auditor, and of the Elective Auditors, which appear on the minutes of the Finance Committee. THE GAS ENGINEERS' REPORT. It was reported that the annual report of the Engineer had been withdrawn at the meeting of the Council owing to differences in the figures relative to salaries, and the Gas Engineer submitted the following explanation : The Annual Report as printed is correct. Previous to this year the costs of wages did not include the salaries paid by cheque, as these are not shown in the wages book. This is an omission which has now been corrected. The correct figures for salaries is given in the cost of gas ; this figure it will be found, does not agree with the wages cost under salaries. Resolved that the explanation be printed, and that the report be again submitted to the council. Resolved that the price of gas within the Borough he reduced by the sum of 2d. per 1,000 feet, as and from the Ist November next. Resolved that Mr. G. McNicoll be appointed assis- tant gas engineer at a salary of £l5O per annum subject to his entering into an agreement to remain in the service of the Corporation for a period of not less than three years. FIRE PRECAUTIONS AT COC.KIIEDGE.

The Fire Engine Committee considered a later from Messrs. Armitage and Rigby, of Cookhodge Mills, pointing out the inadequacy of the water supply there in case of fire, and urging upon the Committee the necessity for at once extending the 8 inch main from Crown-street to the Mill Yard. The Committee resolved that in accordance with the above request the Corporation extend the main from the top of Crown-street to the entrance of the Mills, and that the Borough Surveyor see Messrs. Armitage and Rigby Limited, with a view to their making internal arrangements for fire protection. WATER COMMITTEE.—MR. LAWSON'S CLAIM AMENDED. The Engineer reported that the Specification for the repairs to the "Water Lily" had been approved by Councillors Duncan, Pemberton and Stott on behalf of this Committee. A letter was read from Mr. Lavvson's solicitors for- warding an amended claim against the Corporation in respect of the works at Delph-lane, and giving notice or their intention to apply to the County Court Judge for the appointment of an Arbitrator. Resolved, that in order to enable the claim to be examined Mr. Lawson's solicitors be requested to allow the application to the County Court Judge to lie over for six weeks.

WORKMEN'S FARES. The Tramways Committee has resolved that the Council be recommended to rescind the resolution of 3rd July, relative thereto, and that the following resolution be substituted : " That Id. return tickets be issued before B a.m., and hat the return half remain available on any day during he same week between the hours of 5 and 7 p.m.

div.head: BRA.UTIFUL WARRINGTON SOCIETY. To-day's Show.
div.p: BRA.UTIFUL WARRINGTON SOCIETY. To-day's Show.

The first annual show in connection with the Beautiful Warrington Society will be held in the Parr Hall this (Saturday) afternoon, and promises to be a great success. It will be opened at 2.30 by Colonel R. Ireland Blackburne, C.B, , and will continue until eight o'clock. It is expected that the exhibition will n fford striking evidence of the progress of the movement and of' the interest which is being taken in it by all classes of townspeople. There will be a creditable display of plants and cut flowers, and some of the classes will be specially devoted to school children's exhibits. One of the most pleasing features will be a splendid group of plants grown in the Bank Park Gardens, which will be 10ft. in diameter, and will form a fitting ornament to the centre of the room. The Mayor is sending a choice collection of orchids,and groups of plants (not for competition) will be sent by Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, Mr. and Mrs. T. H. Lyon, Mr. W. Long, and Mrs. Stanton. There will also be some fine collections of cut blooms forwarded by Mr. Vere B. Davies, Mr. Leonard Davies, Mr. Henry Roberts, Mr. F. R. Roberts, Mr. Gordon Roberts, Mr. T. J. Lee, Mrs. Edelsten, Dr. and Mrs. Markel, Mr. John Fairhurst (hon. secretary) and others. Several local nurserymen I will make displays and there will be an interesting exhibit consisting of a section of a beehive. SCHOOL CHILDREN'S COMPETITION. Some two months ago 2,500 plants were distributed to the members of the school children's section of the Society and during the week a competition has been held in 21 out of the 22 schools of the borough. No fewer than 1,190 plants were presented for inspection and prizes were awarded to the children whose exhibits evidenced the most careful tending. First, second, and third prizes and highly commended and com- mended awards were given in respect of each 50 plants. Generally speaking the plants showed that great care had been bestowed upon them and in some schools the judges (Messrs. W. H. Woodcock and J. Ryan) had considerable difficulty in making the awards. In one or two cases the judges were asked to explain why certain plants had not secured•prizes, and this they did, pointing out that some had been over-watered and badly drained whilst others had not been given sufficient moisture. The successful competitors will again show their plants at the Parr Hall to-day (Saturday) in an individual competition, when first, second and third prizes will be given for the best geraniums and similar prizes for the best faschias. Prizes will also be awarded for the best bouquet of wild flowers.

Golborne-street Baptist Bible Class. The annual pic-nic in connection with the above class took place on Saturday last, when about 45 members visited New Brighton. The journey was made by the 1.50 train Central Station, New Brighton being reached by 3.30 when the party went for a short walk. Tea was served at Mrs. Walker's Dining I Rooms, Victoria-road at 4.30, after which the different Ilplaces of amusement were visited including the Tower. I The return journey was made by the 10.50 train from Liverpool, Warrington being reached at 11.30. The outing was voted a success, all having thoroughly enjoyed themselves.

div.head: DEATH OF
div.p: DEATH OF
MR. HENRY TAYLOR, P.C.M.
Sudden End at Douglas.

Warrington people heard with the deepest regret on Monday of the painfully sudden death at Douglas of Mr. Henry Taylor, the esteemed local Police Court Missionary. The news came as a shock for it was only on Saturday that Mr. Taylor, apparently in his usual good health, left Warrington for the Isle of Man to spend a well-earned holiday. He experienced a rough passage but postcards received from him by Warrington friends on Monday morning stated that he had arrived safely and that the weather at Douglas was splendid. Early on Monday there also came the melancholy intimation that Mr. Taylor had passed away, the Chief. Constable (Mr. Luke Talbot) being the recipient of the following telegram : " Douglas. 7.40 a.m. Henry Taylor, 9, Thvnne-street, Warrington, died suddenly. Please tell friends. Superintendent Cain." From the evidence given at the inquest, it appears that Mr. Taylor attended the service at Douglas Head on Sunday afternoon and about six o'clock went for a walk on the Central Promenade. He was seen to make an effort to reach the seats, but staggered and fell to the ground. Several onlookers went to his assistance but he only breathed once or twice afterwards. Heart failure was ' the cause of death. Mrs. Taylor was away at Doncaster when the news of her husband's tragic end reached Warrington. and no time was lost in com- municating the sad tidings to her. Mr. Taylor was one of the best-known figures in Warrington, and his death will mean to many the loss of a true friend. It was amongst the very poorest classes, amid scenes of squalor and poverty, that he pursued what can aptly be described as a noble work. He was a Doncaster man, and came to Warrington about fifteen years ago do undertake the duties of Police Court Missionary. His labours were carried on in the name of the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission of the Church of England Temperance Society —an organization which does much to reclaim the fallen, and to exert an elevating influence on home life. Day after day he was in attendance at the Police Court, and the magistrates were of ten glad to avail themselves of his good offices in cases where there was 'a hope of refor- mation. Many who have stood in the dock have, through his efforts, been given a fresh start in life. Whbre possible work has been found for them and the warm-hearted Police Court Missionary never wearied of encouraging them to keep in the right path. Victims of the -drinking habit have been induced to lamend their ways, and homes which were once the scenes of misery and despair have been made bright and happy. In the part of peace-maker he was ever ready to do his best and he had the satisfaction of bringing about innumerable family reconciliations. He was an indefatigable worker, as is proved by the fact that during the past thirteen years and a half he had paid considerably more than 2,000 visits in War- rington (borough and county), and had seen numerous teetotal pledges taken in homes; taken many boys, girls or women to homes or situations, found for them in a number of cases outfits of clothing to enable them to start well, while in about 150 cases clothing had been given. About 300 cases were attended to at the request of wives, husbands, parents or friends, and most of the disputes were arranged without appearance before the Court. Over 500 letters had been written in respect to cases, and many visits paid to the Manchester gaol to meet prisoners coming out and prevent their going astray again. A hundred and fifty cases had been attended to at the request of magistrates, and in addition to being regularly in his place at the Warrington Police Court Mr. Taylor also acted as Court Missionary at Widnes. Hundreds of persons visited Mr. Taylor's house asking for his advice or assistance, which was, orcourse, always readily given, and frequently a ticket for a night's lodging, food or railway fare, has been provided. Apart from his official duties, Mr. Taylor was ever ready to help on deserving Movements and to shed a ray of sunshine into lives which would otherwise have been almost devoid of pleasure. He was the possessor' of a powerful magic lantern and a splendid set of slides which enabled him to entertain crowds of children in all parts of the town. At the Poor Children's Treat he was always to the fore, sparing no effort to make the day' memorable to the little ones. It did one good to hear the lusty cheers and peals of laughter which his lantern entertainment called forth on these occasions. Mr. Talyor was also a valuable assistant at the hot pot distributions on Christmas Day. Another institution in which he took great interest was the Poor Children's Summer Camp and he was an active member of the Committee. He was a staunch member of the Church of England and had long been associated with the Factory-yard Mission where he was very highly esteemed. Ffis sympathies, however, were with all who tried to uplift the people and to combat the drink evil and he often spoke at Band of Hope and other temperance meetings. He was kindly, genial, and full of feeling for the unfortu• nate and his place will be exceedingly difficult to fill.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Thursday. At the graveside there was a very large attendance of the general public and particularly of that class amongst which Mr. Taylor laboured—a striking evidence of the respect in which the deceased was held in the town. The cortege,headed by a posse of police, left Thynne-street about two o'clock and pro- ceeded to Holy Trinity Church, where a short service was held, conducted by the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton and M. Price. The chief mourners present were Mrs. Taylor (widow), and Mr. J. Taylor (brother), and amongst others present were Mr. Thomas Mr. W. Smith,Mrs. Springit, Mrs. Hunt, Aldermen Bennett and Smethurst. Councillor Clegg, Messrs. T. S. Steel, R. G. Tiolford, W. Gill, W. H. J. Jenkins: J. Harding, .1. W. Hayward. C. A. Bingham, H. Hallard, T. Taker, T. E. Gibson, F. Taylor, S. Taylor. D. Dale, R. Wyllie, the Revs. J. Davies, and H. R. Wild, I Inspector Cox (N.S.P.C.C.), Captain Higson (Church Army), Mr. Bayley, and Mr. Wildman. The C.E.T .8. was represented 133, the Rev. J. Hirst, organis- ing secretary. and Messrs. E. Crawshava, C.E.T.S. clay school, H. Goldston (Liverpool), G. White- hall (Bootle), J. J. Firth (Liverpool),W. Ralphs (Liver- pool) (Police Court Missionaries), T. H. Williams (clerical staff, Liverpool), Mr. Cann (Firewood Factory), Chas. Reid (Wigan), and J. C. Holmes (St. Helens). Amongst the floral tributes placed on the grave nere those from Mr. Taker and family, Mr. and Mrs. T. S. Steel, the C.E.T.S. staff, Rey. and Mrs. J. Hirst, the Factory Yard Mission. and the officers and members of " Charity Tent" of the Independent Order of Rechabites. At the graveside the Rev. J. Hirst paid a high tribute to the many qualities of the deceased. Mr. Taylor was sympathetic and generous in the highest degrae, kind and patient, but above all he ever kept before him the fact that he was a follower of his Lord and Master. He was a staunch Churchman but was a Christian first. Broad in his !sympathies he, without doubt, possessed the confidence of persons of all creeds. In the perform- ance of his duties his first object was ever to help in every way possible those called to his charge,and he did his work to the satisfaction of all. So much was he attached to the work in Warrington that he declined suggestions first that he should go to work in Southport and later that he should join the staff at Liverpool. As a speaker he was earnest end sincere. Mr. Taylor's place On their staff and in Warrington would not be easy to fill. He had been enabled to do much good amongst young men and women in particular and his influence, which had not been confined to mission work, had been great. MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE. Before commencing the business at the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, Mr. Charles White (chair- man) referred to the death of Mr. Henry Taylor, police court missionary. He and his colleagues deeply regretted his demise, as Mr. Taylor frequently came to their assists n ce,and reconciled husband and wife teaching them their duty to themselves and their children. He hoped Mr. Taylor's successor would take an example from a worthy life, and assist the magistrates as he had done. THE WIDOW DESTITUTE. - -

We understand that the widow of the late Mr. Taylor has been left entirely destitute. and that a subscription I;st is to be opened on her behalf. We shall publish further particulars next week. In the meantime Mr. T. S. Steel is acting for Mrs. Taylor.

CROFT ATHLETIC SPORTS: The annual athletic sports in connection with the Croft Horticultural Society were held on Saturday. There was a large crowd of spectators, and the racing generally was of a high order. The arrangements were admirably carried out by the following :—Judges, Messrs. H. Shaw, R. Hodkinson and T. Abbey; starter Mr. Joe Briscoe; handicappers, the Sports Committee ; stewards, Messrs. C. Allen. J. Lodge, R. Ingham, J. Maines, Isaac Maines, and J. Singleton ; hon. secretary, Mr. S. Taylor ; and general secretary, Mr. James Cawthorne. The following were the results :- 110 Yards Boys, Race.-1, H. Robinson, Leigh ; 2 A. Logan, Beswick ; 3, J. Waterworth, Warrington. 110 Yards Flat Race.-1, J. Barber, Beawiek; 2, J. Oakes, Warrington ; 3, J. Bramhall Cadishead. Mile Bicycle Race.-1, S. Spybey, Hels by ; 2, H. Scott, Tarporley ; 3, J. Oakes, Warrington. One Mile Flat Race.-1, J. Robin, Lymm ;2, S. Green, Warrington ; 3, A. Davies, Cadishead. TERRIBLE GUN FATALITY. Mr. W. H. Hackblock, a director of Norwich Brewery and an Alderman of that city, living at the Manor Coltishall, Norfolk, was on Monday standing on the lawn extracting a cartridge from a gun with which he had been shooting rabbits, when it exploded, and the shot struck Mrs. Hackblock in the back of the head, kiUing her instantly. GIRL WIFE ATTEMPTS SUICIDE. At Exmouth on Monday afternoon Blanche Perkins, wife of a sweetmeat vendor, was charged with attempting to commit suicide. Accused, who is only seventeen years of age, and has been married just a month, took salts of lemon, but not sufficient to prove fatal. After some persuasion the husband promised to give her one more chance, and she was discharged.

There is little to be gained by forcing the pace under these conditions, as the balance .of energy will return in dile course after a few ,hours of gentle going. On the whole, however, it is preferable to finish up the daily ride at a point before bodily fatigue becomes marked. Sea Air and Plating.. Every one who takes a bycicle to the seaside will notice how soon the plating is affected' by the salt- laden atmosphere. If a little attention is. paid to the handle-bar and cranks by applying the merest film of vaseline, im serions harm need come to the nickel in the ,Ordinary way. Some seaside local boards indulge in the use of sea-water for sprink- ling the, roads, in which case it is desirable to look after plated rims and spokes. Where, at low water, stretches of firm sand tempt the visitor to indulge in a ride near the sea, it is as well to . remember that particles of damp grit are not likely to enhance the running of the chain. The Child Passenger. With, the number of speedy motor vehicles at present on the road, it should, suggest itself to every thoughtful parent that the practice of carry- ing children of tender age upon the front of bicycles is one fraught with the gravest risks. The health and pleasure which a child may derive from sharing its parent's run into the country is heavily discounted by the helplessness of It position in the event of an unexpected contretemps threaten- ing the stability of the machine. Moreover, even the slight additional weight of the passenger is calculated to disturb the steering of a bicycle, especially under the unfavourable conditions encountered when the rider is compelled to seek the edge of the road, to avoid fast overtaking traffic. Unfortanately the trailer cannot be recommended for safe use on frequented highways, but in secluded districts this adjunct to a cycle certainly offers a solution of the difficulty, pro- vided that moderate speed is observed, and no risks are taken down steep hills.
